The Hydrus (also Enhydros, Enidros, Hildris, Hydra, Hidri, Idra, Idres, Ydre, Ydris and Ydrus) is a creature of Medieval bestiaries.
The hydrus has no fixed look; it is usually taken to be a water snake, but also shown as a bird, a dragon or a mongoose.
Pliny the Elder described the hydrus as an amphibious serpent with venom stronger than any other snake's, whose liver can serve as an antidote to its bite.

In medieval literature the ichneumon or echinemon was the dragon's enemy: on seeing a dragon it coats itself in mud, closes its nostrils with its tail, and attacks and kills the dragon.

Ichneumon (ἰχνεύμων) means 'tracker' in Greek.
According to Pliny the Elder it plunges repeatedly into mud and dries in the sun, and once armed with enough coatings it goes into battle.
According to Strabo, ichneumons wait for crocodiles basking with open mouths, drop into their jaws, and eat through the guts and belly to come out of the dead body.
Strabo records that the people of Heracleopolis worship the ichneumon, the great destroyer of crocodiles and asps.
It is shaped like a ferret but much slimmer, with an elongated head, moves swiftly and can leap a couple of yards in one bound.

According to the French article, through ancient writers such as Pliny the Elder it was linked in medieval European literature with other animals and fought dragons such as the basilisk or the cacatrix.

verified_claims.statement: The kapre is a humanlike mythical creature described as a tall, dark, hairy, muscular tree giant; in Philippine folklore kapres dwell atop fruitless tree branches, smoke large cigars and are mischievous but benign toward travellers.

Kapre comes from Arabic kafir (Spanish cafre), 'non-believer', brought to the Philippines by the Spanish; a synonym is agtà; modern kapre portrayals evolved from racially prejudiced depictions of Negrito tribes by Christianized lowlanders in the Spanish period.
Kapres are believed nocturnal and omnivorous, not necessarily evil, but vengeful if their tree is cut down; a kapre attracted to a woman may follow her throughout life.
Kapres, also called agtà, play pranks, making travellers lose their way in mountains or woods, and can confuse people even in familiar surroundings.
According to Jordan Clark, the name's leading etymology begins with Arabic kāfir, a religious term for an unbeliever, adopted by Portuguese and Spanish as cafre.
Jordan Clark stresses that living Indigenous peoples must not be confused with folklore beings just because colonial accounts used the same name.
The record shows a colonial human label in 19th-century dictionaries, a clearly folkloric kapre in 1906, and traits of regional beings like the pugot being compared or transferred soon after.
Signs of a kapre include rustling branches without strong wind, loud laughter from an unseen being, heavy smoke from a treetop and big red glaring eyes in a tree at night.

Ordinary objects and animals can explain many reported sightings.
Longma is a winged horse bearing dragon scales in Chinese mythology.
Its appearance is regarded as an omen of a sage ruler.
Across the Caribbean and the African diaspora, the Loogaroo, Ligaroo, Lougarou or Lagahoo is a kind of shapeshifter, sorcerer or vampire similar to a werewolf.
The term comes from the French word for werewolf, loup-garou, and is related to the myth of the Soucouyant.
In some myths, like the Soucouyant, the Loogaroo is a witch who sold her soul to the Devil and can shed her skin to become a vampiric fireball called a "corpse candle".
According to these myths she keeps her magic only if she gives the Devil blood every night.
She leaves her skin, usually under a "Devil Tree", a silk cotton tree, and becomes a flame or bright blue ball of light that roams the night seeking blood.
In later versions Loogahoo is a man corrupted by wealth who has made a pact with the Devil to keep his status.
In Haiti the lougawou is a human, usually female, who turns into an animal and drains blood from sleeping victims.
In Trinidad and Tobago the Lagahoo appears at night as a man with a coffin on his neck instead of a head, with three lit candles on top.
To defeat him he must be struck repeatedly with a stick soaked in holy water and holy oils for nine days.
In Mauritian folklore the Lougarou is a notorious figure used mostly to scare children; it appears at full moon and brings trouble to the locals.

Lou Carcolh is a mythical beast of French folklore, a large, slimy, snail-like serpent with hairy tentacles and a big shell, said to live in a cave beneath Hastingues in the Landes, south-west France.
Its slime could sometimes be seen long before it arrived, and its long-reaching tentacles grabbed prey and dragged it into its cave without its leaving.
According to the French article the carcolh is a monstrous snail of Landes folklore peculiar to Hastingues, but references to it are no older than the early 20th century.
By legend the hill that sheltered the town also held a cave housing a carcolh, a fearsome monstrous snail that frightened the inhabitants away and emptied the town.
The legend is encouraged by the hill's rounded shape, like a snail's shell.
The Revue de Gascogne of 1903 mentions a monstrous snail living in a vast, dark cave over which, by tradition, the town of Hastingues is built.
The Russian article says sunlight frightens the snail, so it never comes to the surface.
The Loveland frog is a legendary humanoid creature reportedly seen in Loveland, Ohio, United States.
The legend began with an alleged 1955 sighting and drew renewed attention in 1972, when a Loveland police officer reported meeting an animal like the frogman.
In one story a driver leaving the Branch Hill neighbourhood saw three figures standing on their hind legs by the road.
The figures had leathery skin and frog-like faces; other versions put them on or under a dim bridge, with one holding up a wand that shot sparks.
Loveland police officer Ray Shockey was driving on Riverside Drive near the Little Miami River when an unidentified animal ran across the road in front of him.
He reported that the animal crouched like a frog, then briefly stood upright to climb the guardrail and go back down to the river.
Two weeks later a second Loveland officer, Mark Matthews, saw an unidentified animal crouching by the road in the same area.
According to Matthews, Shockey was shown the dead iguana and confirmed it was the animal he had seen two weeks earlier.
Matthews speculated the iguana was a pet that escaped or was released when it grew too large.

The Shanhaijing locates luan in paradisiacal regions where it sings spontaneously.
The Shuowen Jiezi describes red coloring, five-colored markings, and a chicken-like body.
The Sancai Tuhui calls this bird a transformation of a divine spirit.
The Wakan Sansai Zue says its blood can serve as adhesive for musical-instrument strings.

In Christian mythology, Lucifer is associated with the Devil and a fallen angel.
Lucifer is a name for the morning star, Venus before sunrise.
Isaiah used the day-star expression poetically for the king of Babylon.
In Christian theology, Lucifer became a name for Satan before his fall.
In classical Rome, Lucifer was not typically considered a deity and had few myths.
The Latin name Lucifer means light-bringer and named Venus.
In Roman representations the star was often personified as a torch-bearing male.
The prophetic passage condemns the king of Babylon.
Later Christian interpretation used the name for the devil before his fall.
In the Middle Ages Lucifer became the most popular name.
The interpretation received literary expression in Milton's Paradise Lost.
Roman poetry often portrays Lucifer as heralding dawn.
The name was sometimes also used for Venus as an evening star.
Luduan is an auspicious Chinese legendary creature with a lion head and rhino horn.
Its anatomy combines a dragon body, bear paws, fish scales, and an ox tail.
Luduan is credited with traveling 18,000 li in a day and speaking every language.
Its appearance is associated with enlightened rulers.
The National Palace Museum holds a Luduan-shaped bronze incense burner with gold and silver inlay.
A lugat or liogat is a vampire-like being in Albanian mythology; according to Orel the word "lugat" is borrowed from Vulgar Latin *lupus peccatus ("false wolf"), though the semantics are difficult.
They dwell in shadows and darkness, especially places never touched by sunlight, such as wells, old ruins and caves; they have a frightening face and are extremely violent.
A lugat can fly and ride the winds, attacks its victims in their sleep, and lures people, especially children, while hidden in darkness.
As undead they cannot be killed at night, but if caught in their graves they can be burnt to death; lugats are often believed to wear a dead person's skin and to have long fingernails.
In Albanian the word llugat is also used for a wicked or frightening person.
The lugat is a figure of Albanian mythology described by Arshi Pipa as "a tormented soul that the earth casts out because of some grave wrongdoing".
In Kosovo it is believed that a dead person also rose as a lugat if no gun barrel, fire tongs, sickle or other iron was placed beside them, since iron apparently keeps all spirits away.
Hahn adds that among the northerners he met, Christians never rose as lugats, whereas among southerners there was no religious distinction in becoming a lugat.
In the original myth, as the seventh child of Tau and Kerana he was the most accursed, looking like a giant, hideous dog.
The myth says a family's seventh son will transform on his 13th birthday.
The maned wolf, a slender long-legged wolf-like canid with a shambling gait, fitted the werewolf image brought by settlers and was eventually blended with local Guarani myths.

Since the 19th century the President of Argentina has customarily been godparent to every seventh son, a custom born because superstitious people sometimes sacrificed their seventh son for fear he was a Luisón.
On 12 March 1973 President Juan Domingo Perón made the custom law through Decree No. 848, the presidential sponsorship law.
According to the Spanish article, as the seventh son of Tau and Keraná he bears his parents' heaviest curse; his very name terrifies, and he stands at the crossroads of life and death.
According to the Portuguese article it is believed to look like a South American wolf or a red-eyed monkey, with fish fins and a huge tapir-like phallus.
On full-moon nights falling on Friday and/or Tuesday the person turned into a half-animal creature.
Lukwata is a legendary water-dwelling creature in Baganda folklore in Lake Victoria in Uganda.
It is described as 20–30 feet long with dark smooth skin and rounded head, attacking fishermen and boats.
Pieces of Lukwata were thought to have magical properties and revered as relics.
Lukwata remains an important part of the cultural identity of the Baganda people in Uganda.
Colonial administrator C. W. Hobley recorded in 1913 that people around Lake Victoria told stories of Lukwata.
Its folklore may have been related to spirits and deities surrounding canoes and fishing.
In Caribbean folklore the Lusca is a sea monster said to live around the blue holes near Andros, an island in the Bahamas.
The first report resembling the Lusca came in 1872, when J. S. George of Nassau wrote to the American Naturalist about a "colossal octopus" found dead on the beach.
Marine biologist Bruce S. Wright was told by a local guide that limestone caves under a lake were home to the lusca, a large half-octopus, half-dragon animal with sucker-tipped tentacles.
Lusca is a clipped form of Mollusca, referring to the creature's mollusc features such as tentacles.
It is described as a giant octopus, a giant cuttlefish, or half shark, half octopus.
The St. Augustine monster found on the Florida coast in 1896 is considered one of the best candidates for a lusca specimen.
A lutin is a kind of hobgoblin (an amusing goblin) in French folklore and fairy tales.
In Norman folklore it plays a role like the household spirits of England, Germany and Scandinavia.
It sometimes appears as a saddled horse ready to ride, and in this form is called Le Cheval Bayard.
Lutins sometimes tangle the hair of people or horses into elf-locks.
The French fairy tale Le Prince Lutin was written in 1697 by Marie Catherine d'Aulnoy.
In that tale the lutin can become invisible at will, cross the universe in a moment and rise without wings.
The name is attested as netun around 1176–1181 by Chrétien de Troyes in Yvain, the Knight of the Lion.
It comes from Latin Neptunus, the Roman sea god's name, which in Late Latin also came to mean a pagan god.
Belief in lutins spread to North America, especially Quebec in Canada, as spirits in the form of pets or other common animals.
Completely white cats are especially thought likely to be lutins.
The lutin is a small nocturnal humanoid from the folklore of French regions such as Berry, Normandy and Picardy.
The Ardennes and Wallonia know a very similar household spirit called the nuton.
Lutzelfrau is documented as saint lucy shrouded in regional lore.
Ly Erg is documented as fairy scottish folklore in regional lore.
Lyngbakr is documented as lyngbakr icelandic lyngi in regional lore.

Some say ma bong has a horse's lower body and a man's upper body, the spirit of men who never had partners; some that it is a dead horse's spirit that nibbles dried buffalo heads; others give it a beautiful woman's upper body that lures and kills young men.
Despite variations, ma bong is always associated with horses; its presence brings neighing and galloping, and it vanishes leaving only horse tracks.
In the Lanna tale, a young man follows his friend and sees him hungrily licking a buffalo's head; a Buddhist monk advises him to smear it with chilli.

Chased by his friend, now a red-eyed spirit, the man throws raw eggs that the hungry spirit stops to eat, then turns his staircase upside down; the spirit cannot climb, and he sees his friend has become a horse-bodied ma bong.
Others say ma bong has a horse's lower body and a beautiful woman's upper body, luring young men before killing them.
Maa-alused is documented as alused estonian folk in regional lore.
Madam Koi Koi is a Nigerian urban legend of a vengeful ghost in boarding schools in Ghana and Nigeria.
She is often depicted wearing a pair of red heels or a single heel.
She is one of the most popular boarding school ghosts in Nigeria.
The name Madam Koi Koi is taken from the sound her heels make when preying on students.
In Nigeria, she was depicted as a stylish secondary school teacher known for her red heels.
Her shoes produced a koi koi sound in the hallways from which her name originated.
Madam Pigott is documented as madam pigott madam in regional lore.
The Madre de aguas ("Mother of water"), also known as Magüi, is a mythical creature of Cuban folklore.
In Creole folklore she is Mama Glo; on other islands she is Mami Wata or Watramama.
The story, first told in the 1600's, says she is a giant boa as thick as a palm tree.
She has two horn-like projections on her head and thick scales impenetrable to bullets.
She inhabits rivers and lakes, which never dry while she lives there.
The Madre de aguas never dies, and anyone who tries to kill or capture her dies.
A shrine to Nak was built at Wat Mahabut and in 1997 relocated to Suan Luang district, Bangkok.
While Nak was pregnant, Mak was sent to war and seriously wounded.
Nak stretched her arm to an impossible length to pick up a lime, and Mak realized she was a ghost; he then fled to Wat Mahabut, which ghosts cannot enter.
Grieving, Nak terrorized Phra Khanong; a powerful monk captured her ghost, sealed it in an earthen jar and threw it into the canal.
In another version, the monk assured Nak she would be reunited with her husband in a future life, so she willingly departed.
Devotees bring offerings with requests, usually women seeking easy childbirth or their husband's exemption from conscription.
The legend, believed to date to the early Rattanakosin period, says Mae Nak lived near Wat Mahabut beside a canal.
Nak became a pee tai tang klom (ghost of a woman who died in childbirth with the baby inside); out of love her spirit stayed bound to her old life, appearing in human form to do the housework.
Somdej Toh cremated Nak's body and carved out a piece of her forehead bone to keep as an amulet.
The story also illustrates Buddhist teachings on samsara and the three marks of existence.
Prince Damrong recalled asking Wat Phra Kaeo visitors as a child who was most popular, and most answered Mae Nak.
In Thai folklore ghosts fear sticky Blumea leaves, so Mak hid behind a Blumea balsamifera bush.
In other versions, the monk Somdet Phra Phutthachan (To Phrommarangsi) defeats Nak by confining her spirit in her forehead bone, bound to his waistband.
Maelor Gawr is documented as maelor gawr early in regional lore.
In Māori tradition, the Maero (or Mohoao) are an iwi-atua or supernatural people from New Zealand.
They are described as giants or wild men inhabiting mountains and forests in the South Island and Tararua Range.
Maero are characterised as wild, malevolent and violent, carrying stone clubs as weapons.
They are covered in dark body hair and have long bony fingers with sharp fingernails.
The Maero harbor anger towards the Māori from Hawaiki for displacing them.
Tukoio attacked a maero, cutting off its arms, legs and head.
The head brought back was still alive and called for help.
The maero put itself back together and returned to the forest.
Maggy Moulach is documented as maggy moulach known in regional lore.
Maha Sona is a yaksha or demon of Sinhalese folklore in Sri Lanka.
His name is interpreted as the greatest demon or god or demon of the cemetery.
One version identifies his origin as the warrior Ritigala Jayasena, defeated in a duel with Gotaimbara.
In that version a deity attaches a bear's head to revive him.
Folk songs contain origins not always connecting him with Jayasena.
He is believed to haunt graveyards, large rocks, hills and three-road junctions.
Mahishi is a demoness in Hindu mythology whose story concerns Ayyappa and Sabarimala.
This source calls her the sister of the buffalo demon Mahishasura.
She receives a boon that only a child of Shiva and Vishnu's union can kill her.
Ayyappan's birth satisfies that condition through Shiva's union with Mohini, Vishnu's female manifestation.
Ayyappan seizes her horns and casts her to Earth during their battle.
Kerala Tourism explains Ayyappa's birth mission as eliminating the threat posed by Mahishi.
Mahoraga are a group of reptilian deities in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions.
Depictions can have reptilian bodies from the waist down.
They belong to eight classes of deities protecting the Dharma.
They are described as huge underground serpents rotating the earth and sometimes causing earthquakes.
They are also associated with instrumental music.
It serves as the mount of Ganga, Narmada, and Varuna.
Makaras are regarded as guardians of gateways and thresholds of temples and throne rooms.
The Sanskrit word makara means sea animal or crocodile.
Its common form combines a terrestrial animal's front with an aquatic animal's rear.
In Sinhalese artwork a makara combines parts of several animals such as elephant trunk and crocodile jaws.
Makuragaeshi is a Japanese spirit or yōkai.
It is said to turn over a sleeper’s pillow at night.
Other accounts have it reverse the position of a sleeper’s head and feet.
Its appearance varies, sometimes resembling a child or monk.
An Edo-period illustration depicts a miniature Niō guardian.
An origin story makes it the ghost of someone who died in the room.
Malingee is a nocturnal malignant Australian Aboriginal spirit.
In Aboriginal mythology they avoid humans but when provoked slay mercilessly with a stone knife or axe.
Malingees have stone knees that knock making a scraping sound, and eyes that smolder like coals.
These features made it possible for humans to detect and avoid nearby Malingees.
Mama D'Leau derives from French meaning Mother of the River, known also as Mama Dlo and Mama Glo.
She protects and heals river animals in Saint Lucia, Trinidad and Tobago, and Dominica.
Depicted as a beautiful woman whose body twists into coils below the waist.
Mamlambo is a deity in South African and Zulu mythology, the goddess of rivers, described as a large snake-like creature.
In 1997, South African newspapers reported sightings of a giant reptile monster in the Mzintlava River near Mount Ayliff.
Villagers claimed the creature was about 20 meters long, had the head of a horse, and shined with green light at night.
For this reason, the Mamlambo is often referred to as the Brain Sucker.
The Manaia is a mythological creature in Māori culture, common in carving and jewellery.
The Manaia is usually depicted with bird head, fish tail, and human body.
The Manaia is believed to be the messenger between mortals and spirits, and a guardian against evil.
In this form it is represented in a figure-of-eight shape culminating in a bird-like beak.
Related Manaia-like symbols are found in other Polynesian cultures such as Hawaii.
Manaia designs are often depicted three-fingered representing birth, life, and death.
The manananggal is a mythical creature of Philippine folklore said to detach its upper torso from its lower body; its fangs and wings give it a vampire-like look.
Manananggál derives from Tagalog tanggál ('to remove', 'to separate'), literally 'remover' or 'separator', interpretable as 'one who separates itself'.

In Philippine folklore the manananggal is usually a fearsome creature, most often female, that separates its upper body, revealing its entrails, and grows large bat-like wings to fly at night in search of victims.
The manananggal is believed to prey on sleeping pregnant women with a long proboscis-like tongue to extract fetuses or draw blood.

Folklore also links it with newlyweds, lovers and newborns; while it hunts, its lower torso stays motionless and is its weak point, and it is killed by applying salt, garlic, ash or fire to that lower half.
The manananggal myth is widely known in the Visayas, especially Capiz, Iloilo, Bohol and Antique.
Manananggals are believed to be repelled by garlic, salt and holy water, and to avoid daggers, light, vinegar, spices and a stingray's tail.
Comparable mythical figures appear in neighbouring Southeast Asian cultures, including Indonesia and Malaysia.
Plasencia recorded the magtatangal, which showed itself at night to many people without its head or entrails.
Domingo de los Santos's dictionary (1703) says the magtatangal flies and eats human flesh with only half its body, hence its name from tangal, 'to disengage'.
Plasencia thought it a fable, though locals said they had seen it; this occurred in Catanduanes.
That description is from Fray Domingo de los Santos, Vocabulario de Lengua Tagala (1703).
If it fails to recombine before sunrise, the creature is believed to die.
The manananggal was hypothesized to explain sudden miscarriages in ancient Philippines.
The magtatangal account is from Fr. Juan de Plasencia, Customs of the Tagalogs (1589).
The manananggal is generally associated with traits similar to other folkloric beings such as vampires, Visayan entities and aswangs.
Manannán mac Lir is documented as manann known warrior in regional lore.
The Manaul (also Manaol) is a Philippine folklore bird with at least four stories; the name is also the common name of two large Philippine eagles, the Philippine eagle and white-bellied sea eagle.
A Manaul bird is mentioned in the Code of Kalantiaw from Panay, which makes killing it punishable by death.
In Mangyan and Negrito folklore, Manaul was a wrathful king imprisoned by King Tubluck Lawi; escaping, he rebelled against the gods, and the rocks Kaptan threw at him missed and became islands.

In Tagalog folklore, Bathala sent a tigmamanukan omen bird named Manaul to peck the bamboo; it split open, releasing the first man, Malakas, and the first woman, Maganda; Manaul then flew right to left as a good omen; other sources say Amihan in bird form pecked it.
Historians now generally accept that the Code of Kalantiaw documents appear to be deliberate fabrications, written in 1913 by Jose Marco.

According to Jordan Clark, the Pavón manuscripts' trail leads to the 20th-century forger José E. Marco; the Manaul story is worth reading as folklore history, but the manuscript cannot authenticate it as ancient Visayan.
The fullest named Manaul account comes through the so-called Pavón manuscripts.
Mande Barung is an alleged apelike creature said to inhabit Meghalaya forests in the Garo Hills.
It is generally described as a large, hairy, bipedal hominoid.
According to Pliny the Elder, the Mandi are a short-lived people from India.
Pliny equates the Mandi, named by Cleitarchus and Megasthenes, whose women can bear children at seven and grow old at forty, with the Macrobii.
Pliny also says Agatharchides describes them as living on locusts and being swift-footed.
The mandurugo is a mythical being of Philippine folklore similar to a vampire.
The mandurugo, a variety of aswang, is usually a young beautiful woman by day but at night grows wings and a long sharp tongue to cut a man's neck or prick his mouth while kissing to get blood.
Its stories, popular among Tagalog and Bicol speakers, vary; sometimes it marries men to prey on them, or keeps one husband as cover and flies to other villages to feed.
In The Girl With Many Loves, the fourth husband keeps a knife, feels a prick on his neck, stabs the creature above him, and next day his wife is found dead with a knife wound in her chest.
Maní is a Tupi mythological character, a very fair-skinned girl whose story forms a Tupi origin myth.
The Amazonian legend of Maní is tied to the cult of manioc, the staple food that grew from her grave.
In Canadian folklore, Manipogo is a lake monster said to live in Lake Manitoba, Canada.
The creature was named Manipogo in 1960, echoing British Columbia's Ogopogo.
It is described as having a brownish-black body with at least one hump showing above the water.
Its head is likened to a horse's, camel's or sheep's, while others say it is flat and diamond-shaped.
It reportedly shrieks or cries as it surfaces.
Local First Nations people have legends of serpent-like creatures in Lake Manitoba going back hundreds of years.
The first documented sighting by a white settler was in September 1909, when Hudson's Bay Company fur trader Valentine McKay claimed to see a huge creature.
Some sceptics think the monster is a swimming moose with its head and humped back showing.
In 1936 fisherman Oscar Fredrickson found an animal skull in his fishing net.
Soon after, Fredrickson's house burned down for unknown reasons and the skull was lost.
Local indigenous people also have legends of a water monster; according to this source, the creature was named Manipogo in 1957, echoing British Columbia's Ogopogo.
Manohara is a kinnari, a bird woman, and heroine of a Jataka tale.
Her story appears in the Pannasa Jataka, Divyavadana, and Borobudur reliefs.
She is the youngest of the Kinnara king's seven daughters living on Kailash.
A hunter captures her and gives her to Sudhana, who later marries her.
When accused of bringing misfortune and threatened with death she flies home, leaving a ring and directions for Sudhana.
Sonobudoyo explains that Manohara on Borobudur reliefs is depicted as a complete human resembling an angel.
The manticore is a Persian man-eating monster with a lion’s body and a human face.
The name manticore is traced to a Persian word for man-eater.
The manticore also appears in medieval bestiaries.
The quoted account of Ctesias gives it three rows of teeth, human ears, and light-blue eyes.
That account depicts a scorpion-like tail with a long sting.
Pausanias writes that he is inclined to think the reported creature is a tiger.
The manticore is believed to inhabit lonely places outside communities.
Manussiha is a Burmese mythical creature half human and half lion.
The legend associates its creation by monks with protecting a royal baby from sea ogresses.
Guardian statues stand at the four angles around a pagoda.
The creature combines a human upper body and head with leonine hindquarters.
Its Pali name combines manussa, human, and siha, lion.
The French source recounts monks creating a thousand man lion figures to repel ogresses.
The Mapinguari is often described as an extremely foul-smelling, hairy animal that is distinct from the North American Bigfoot.

Descriptions further allege that the cryptid is a man-eating creature with hook-shaped nails, backwards-facing feet, a bipedal gait, a gaping mouth in its abdomen, and a single eye like the mythological Cyclops.
The creature's size has been depicted as either comparable to a human, or larger.
The other recurring feature of the Mapinguari is a large, single eye in either the abdomen or the forehead, like a Cyclops.
The marabbecca is a legendary creature from Sicily, its name probably of Arabic origin; it lives in wells and reservoirs, looks like a woman or an amphibian and moves only at night.
It is thought to have been invented by Sicilian parents to keep children from playing near wells.
According to the Italian article, the creature lives in wells and cisterns and was invented by Sicilian mothers to scare children away from the dangers of an open well.
The Macedonian article also says it is of Arabic origin, lives in wells and reservoirs, looks like a woman and moves only at night.
Margot the fairy is, in the traditions of Brittany and the Mayenne, the generic name of certain earthly fairies, best known in central Brittany, especially the Côtes-d'Armor.
Probably descended from the fairy Morgana and, before her, from an aspect of Mother Earth, the Margot fairies are powerful: they can turn invisible, change shape and transform others.

They are fine dancers, often generous and sometimes cruel, who enjoy testing humans with gifts of gold and objects, are believed to have built several monuments and to hide great treasure underground, and keep animals, often cattle.
Tales tell how they steal human children, leaving their own in their place, and become godmothers of babies whom they name and endow with more or less useful gifts.
They reward the righteous and punish those who harm them or are greedy or indiscreet with them, and sometimes steal.
According to the French article, many megaliths and rocks are said to be these fairies' homes or their furniture and tools: table, spindle, room, clog, armchair, cradle.
They were the object of cults, especially at the Margot cave; until the end of the 19th century these beliefs led many people to sacrifice animals to them and hunt for their treasures.
The name probably distorts that of Morgana, the famous fairy of Arthurian myth; in Lower Brittany they were first called Morgana.
Roger Sherman Loomis sees a link between the fairies of Upper Brittany and the Morgain of the Arthurian romances.
The Spanish article also calls Margot the fairy the generic name of certain earthly fairies in the traditions of Brittany and the Mayenne.
A marid is a type of devil in Islamic tradition.
The Arabic word marid means rebellious and applies to these supernatural beings.
Hans Wehr’s dictionary defines marid as demon or giant.
MacNaghten’s edition of One Thousand and One Nights treats marid and ifrit as interchangeable terms.
In Amira El-Zein’s account, marid tries to predict the future by ascending to heaven and eavesdropping on angels.
As-Saffat 37:7 uses the phrase every rebellious devil, cited for the adjective marid.
Marmennill is documented as scandinavian folklore marmennill in regional lore.
In Lleida, Lo Marraco is known as a dragon-sized lizard with a very wide mouth that eats babies' dummies, as a symbol of their growing up.
Lo Marraco is also a traditional child-scarer of Lleida; the same name (as marreco) was used to frighten children elsewhere, such as the Maestrat and Menorca.
According to the Spanish article, the Marraco is a totem animal of Lérida dating from the 5th century BC, freely represented.

The Catalan article stresses that these ancient-origin conjectures, and the idea that the name comes from Basque for 'dragon', have no historical or scientific basis; the totem animal of the Ilergetes was the wolf, not the dragon.
A recorded precursor of Lo Marraco de Lleida was the dragon figure the city used in the procession of the Assumption of Mary in 1551.
Marțolea is documented as demonic entity romanian in regional lore.
Maruda is a female demon of Slavic mythology said to harass children in the cradle.

In the 19th century magical methods were thought necessary to deal with the demon, for example putting three spindles, three spoons and sewing into a bowl of water to keep the harasser busy so the baby could sleep undisturbed.
Maruda (also meaning a dull, grumbling, sluggish, tiresome person) is a demonic female figure who torments children in cradles, keeping them from sleep and making them cry.
In the room where the baby slept, a bowl of water holding a ball of thread, a spoon and a spindle was placed; busy with these things, the demon left the child in peace.
People also made nine rag dolls and placed them around the baby's cradle, starting at the head end.
In some parts of the Lublin region girls were forbidden to play with dolls, since a maruda that strangles children was thought to sit in them.
A matagot is a spirit of French folklore that usually takes the form of a black cat.
Matagots are generally evil, but some help, like the 'magician cat' that brings wealth to a home if well fed.
A wealth-bringing matagot must be lured with a fresh plump chicken and carried home without its new owner looking back.
If the cat gets the first mouthful of food and drink at every meal and is well treated, it brings good luck; a matagot can serve up to nine masters at once.
In Gascon tradition one must not keep the matagot for life: a dying owner suffers a long agony until he frees it.

According to the French article, the chat d'argent, mandragot or matagot of Breton, Gascon, Provençal and Languedoc folklore is a usually black, diabolical cat a sorcerer obtains in exchange for his soul.
It roams mysterious places at night and returns at dawn with gold louis for its master; if neglected or unrewarded it takes offence and may take cruel revenge.
Sometimes the cat serves nine masters and leads the last to hell.
The Catalan article calls the matagot, also mantagot, a spirit of Occitan mythology known especially in Provence and Languedoc.

verified_claims.statement: In Māori mythology, Matuku-tangotango is an ogre who kills Wahieroa son of Tāwhaki.
In some versions, Matuku lives in a cave called Putawarenuku.
Matuku's servant reveals that at the new moon his master can be killed at his washing pool.
When the new moon arrives, Rātā grabs the ogre by the hair at the pool and kills him.
Maushop is a mythical hero and giant in Wampanoag folklore.
Legend recounts he came from Aquinnah on Martha's Vineyard before the tribe's arrival.
Maushop was considered a tribal provider who taught hunting and fishing.
Mavka is documented as mavka ukrainian nyavka in regional lore.
They are shown as a cross between apes and homunculi with grey fur, also like cats or monkeys, wearing a distinctive red cap they need for their mischief.
The mazapégul are blamed for nightmares, including sleep paralysis and choking sensations, tousling sleeping women's hair, stomach aches, vanishing objects, clashing cymbals and flying dishes.
In the countryside they bother animals, especially horses, which wake sweating with braided tails and manes.
Drawn to pretty girls, they enter their rooms at night, fall asleep on their stomachs and praise them: 'What beautiful eyes! What beautiful hair!'
If its cap is stolen or thrown down the well, the thief may be pestered at night with the cry 'give me back my cap!'
Grains of rice scattered on a windowsill keep the mazapégul busy counting them until daybreak.

The mazapégul descend from the incubus, a demon that troubled sleepers and preyed on women, and share traits with elves elsewhere, such as the Laurieddhu of southern Italy and those of the French Vosges.
Mazapégul lore is recorded in Giuliano Fantaguzzi's survey of early 15th-century Cesena.
According to the Spanish article, the family name is first recorded in an extract of a sales contract of 9 May 1487 in the General Archive of Forlì.
The Italian article also calls the Mazapégul a sprite (folletto) of the folk tradition of Romagna, especially the Forlì Apennines.
The term has been applied to figures in several religious traditions.
It can refer generally to demons and other threatening beings.
Mazomba is a giant fish in the mythology of the Chaga people of Tanzania.
It is also the name of a crater on Triton, a moon of Neptune.
Mazomba was documented in The Mythology of All Races edited by Louis Herbert Gray.
The crater is listed in the Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.
The crater feature is registered with the USGS Astrogeology Research Program.
Encyclopedia documentation of this African myth is categorized as a concise stub.
Mbielu-mbielu-mbielu is a cryptid seen at the Likouala River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
It has green planks growing out of its back, leading to suggestions of an extant stegosaurid.
It is usually submerged with only its back showing, covered in green algal growths.
Mbwiri is a Central African demon said to possess people.
Those he possesses would usually be diagnosed with epilepsy by a doctor.
When such a possession occurs, a shaman is summoned.
A hut is built where the afflicted resides with the shaman until cured.
Mbwiri is said to abhor good living and merrymaking, making this the best way to drive him out.
When cured, he builds a little fetish house and avoids certain foods.
Medjed is an Egyptian sacred elephantfish worshipped at Oxyrhynchus.
In the myth, the fish swallows Osiris’s penis after Set scatters his body parts.
Meduza (Russian folklore) is documented as meduza russian meluza in regional lore.
Dragons feature in Meitei stories, literature, mythology and religion in Manipur.
Khelchandra Singh describes Pakhangba as the god king of Manipur in local belief.
In that account he can move as a dragon at night.
Manipur's kings use the dragon image as royal insignia.
In the folklore of Ohio, Michigan and Connecticut, melon heads are large-headed humanoids who sometimes emerge from hiding to attack people.
Different versions give them different origins.
One Michigan story says they were children with hydrocephalus at the Junction Insane Asylum near Felt Mansion.
The Allegan County Historical Society says the asylum never existed.
In Canadian folklore, Memphré is a lake monster said to live in Lake Memphremagog between Newport, Vermont, and Magog, Quebec.
Memphré is often described much like the Loch Ness Monster.
Menehune are a mythological dwarf-like race in Hawaiian lore living in deep forests.
Menehune are superb craftspeople credited with building heiau, fishponds, roads, and canoes.
Some structures attributed to the Menehune still exist today.

In Finnish mythology and lore the menninkäinen were originally described as spirits living in isolated places and generally friendly to humans; over time the term evolved and the menninkäinen came to be described as goblin-like creatures.
These creatures are believed to resemble leprechauns, guarding treasures and enjoying riddles and games of dominance.
Sources disagree on where menninkäinen live: some call them "industrial workers" in urban settings, others forest dwellers.
Merfolk, Mercreatures, Mermen or Merpeople are legendary water-dwelling, human-like beings.
In English, female merfolk are called mermaids appearing half-woman and half-fish; male merfolk are called mermen.
Merfolk in the Philippines are known collectively as Taga-Dagat or Bantay Tubig.
The most famous persona of merfolk is the Sirena with a human female upper body and fish tail.
Sireno is the male counterpart of Sirena.
A mermaid is a mythical sea being with a woman's upper body and a fish tail.
Mermaid stories span cultures around the world.
Some traditions link mermaids to sea fertility and others to danger for sailors.
Southeast Asian tales include the mermaid princess Suvannamaccha.
Early Greek sirens were woman-bird beings often confused with mermaids.
Reported dugong sightings have been associated with mermaids.
Folkloric mermaids have a woman's upper body and fish tail.
Suvannamaccha’s tale involves Hanuman trying to build a stone bridge across the sea.
Mermaid of Warsaw is documented as polish syrenka cognate in regional lore.
Merrow is documented as merrow irish middle in regional lore.
Mhachkay is a creature of Turkic, especially Tatar, mythology somewhat like a vampire.
A person born with two hearts and two souls was thought to be a Mhachkay and, once recognised, was driven from human settlements.
Mhachkays were usually people who died young; only one soul departed, and the other revived the corpse to prey on the living.
These undead fly at night as owls, attacking night travellers and people who stray into the woods, sucking their blood and eating their insides.
When a known Mhachkay dies, beheading the corpse and burying the head apart is said to stop it rising again.
Like Nosferatu, the məçkəy is believed to carry tağun, the plague.
It is imagined as a hunched old woman spreading death, sometimes an old man.
In Mongolian məç means monkey, while məs means weapon.
Miage-nyūdō is a yōkai of Sado Island.
It is classified as a kind of mikoshi-nyūdō.
The figure grows taller when a traveler looks up at it.
A Hamochi version steals travelers’ food and money.
An Utami account associates it with a stone that changes form.

In folklore the Michigan Dogman is an alleged creature first seen in 1887 in Wexford County, Michigan, United States, described as a seven-foot (2.1 m), blue- or amber-eyed two-legged canine with a man's torso and a howl like a human scream.
Folklore says the creature reappears every ten years, in years ending in seven.
After he played the song, Cook got calls from listeners who said they had met a similar creature.
According to the French article, the Dogman is a two-legged dog-like animal of Michigan folklore born of a 1987 local song, possibly echoing older tales.
According to Cook a Native legend has the dogman roaming the Manistee River since Odawa times, though no authentic source has ever been documented.
According to the Russian article, cryptozoological literature classes the dogman as an alleged upright canid, while folklorists see it mainly as a figure of modern regional legend.
Mikoshi-nyūdō is a long-necked yōkai resembling a bald monk.
Edo-period ghost tales describe it startling people.
Some accounts place its sudden appearance on roads at night.
In some stories looking up at it can endanger a traveler.
The Milton Lizard is described as a 15-foot monitor lizard sighted in Cable Creek near Milton.
First sighted in July by Clarence Cable in a wrecking yard north of Milton.
He watched the lizard crawl from behind vehicle wrecks, hissing repeatedly.
Mimis are fairy-like beings of Arnhem Land in northern Australian Aboriginal folklore.
Mimis have elongated thin bodies and live in rock crevices to avoid snapping in wind.
Mimis painted the first rock art before Aboriginal people first arrived in northern Australia.
Minairons come from St John's-wort, which blooms on St John's Night (the summer solstice), grows in very deep caves guarded by giants and dragons, and can only be taken at midnight on St John's Day.
Some say they are like a swarm of tiny, almost invisible mosquitoes; others compare them to bees for the buzzing they make leaving the needle case.
They are so tiny that thousands fit in the case, and when they come out they demand work, saying, 'What shall we do? What shall we say?'
Legend says many of the Pyrenean screes are their work, made when a master opened the needle case by mistake.
A few heirs of great Pyrenean houses reputedly owned the case, through which their house rose like a mushroom.
According to the Spanish article, when the case was opened, if the opener did not set them work at once, the minairons killed him.
According to the French article, the Basque counterpart, mamarro or mamarroak, are small spirits who help with daily tasks and protect the family they live with.
These little elves are also called Galtzagorriak, Prakagorriak and Zaingorriak at Ordizia, among other names.
The Minhocão is a creature of Brazilian folklore variously said to be a large fish or worm-like.
Locals in Brazil described the Minhocão to European explorers and naturalists in the 19th century.
French naturalist Augustin Saint-Hilaire recorded in December 1846 accounts of Minhocão in the Padre Aranda and Feia lakes that often dragged horses and cattle under water.
He concluded that Minhocão is an augmentative of minhoca, Portuguese for earthworm.
Saint-Hilaire guessed it might be a large species of South American lungfish.
It was also reported by German naturalist Fritz Müller in a German scientific journal in 1878.
It was said to uproot trees, leave deep trenches in its path and prefer damp conditions.
Cryptozoologist Karl Shuker suggested a link with the Sachamama, a cryptid of Peru.
The Minka or Minka Bird is an owl-like bird in Ngarrindjeri stories along the Murray River.
The Minka foretold death, whereas the similar mulduwanke stole children.
Both were believed to live in dark recesses.
Minnie Quay is an apparition of notable interest in Michigan paranormal lore.
Lore dictates that one must leave something on her tombstone or she will follow them home.
Her ghost has been reported roaming the beaches of Forester.

The minokawa is a giant dragon-like bird of Philippine mythology; early people believed it could swallow or cover the sun, causing eclipses; it lives in outer space, can devour the sun and moon, and would try the earth too.
In a Bagobo tale the minokawa is an island-sized bird with sword feathers, mirror eyes and steel-like beak and legs, living outside the sky at the eastern horizon.
The moon makes eight holes in the east to come out and eight in the west to go in, because each day the big bird tries to catch her.

When the moon is in the bird's belly and the sky is dark, the Bagobo scream, cry and beat gongs, fearing being eaten; the racket makes the minokawa look down and open its mouth, and the moon jumps out and runs away.

An early dictionary locates the creature in lakes and rivers.
One explanation links its name with the Japanese term mizuchi.
Stories of Mistapew are current in Indigenous North American traditional and popular culture in the twenty-first century.
Mixtecatl is one of the six giant sons of Iztac-Mixcoatl and Tlaltecuhtli (or Ilancueitl) who populated the Earth after the Great Flood in the Fifth Sun of Aztec mythology.
He was the fifth son, founder of Mixtlan, origin of the people of the region now called Mixteca.
Some commentators interpret it as a water deity.
The name appears in the Nihon Shoki and a Man’yōshū poem.
One analysis divides its old pronunciation into elements for water, possession and spirit.
The metal eating description comes from Guo Pu's commentary rather than the early Shan Hai Jing text itself.
The Mobile Wolf Woman is a legendary creature reported to live in Mobile, Alabama, United States.
Reports described seeing a creature with the body of a wolf and the head of a woman.
Witnesses described the creature with a woman's upper half and a wolf's lower half.
Moddey Dhoo is documented as moddey dhoo manx in regional lore.

verified_claims.statement: The moehau is a creature in New Zealand folklore reputed to live on Coromandel Peninsula's Moehau.
Some Māori suggest it descends from maero wild men, while another theory posited an escaped baboon.
The Mogollon Monster, also called the Arizona Bigfoot, is an ape-like creature reported along the Mogollon Rim in central and eastern Arizona.
It is usually described as a large biped over 7 feet tall with large red eyes.
Anecdotal reports say it is nocturnal, omnivorous, territorial and sometimes violent.
Many reports say it gives a blood-curdling scream like a woman in great distress.
The Mohan or Poira is a name applied to several supernatural creatures in South and Central American folklore.
Various legends exist about the Mohan, many emerging from Colombia.
The Mohan is known as an avatar whose form can be adopted by shamans.
In several Bantu mythologies, Mokele-mbembe is a mythical water-dwelling entity believed to exist in the Congo River Basin.
It is described as a reptilian creature, a spirit, or an extinct sauropod.
In the early to mid-20th century, the entity became a focus of cryptozoology and young Earth creationism.
First attested in 1913 in the Republic of the Congo, Africa.
The quest for the creature is seen as an attempt to challenge the theory of evolution.
Researchers noted that the seekers of Mokele-mbembe are creationists rather than wildlife biologists.
Mokoi is an evil spirit in Yolngu Aboriginal lore who killed sorcerers practicing black magic.
The Murngin believed deaths resulted from disease or accidents caused by a mokoi.
Momo is a large, hairy humanoid creature reportedly sighted in rural Missouri.
Witnesses alleged the creature resembles a bipedal ape standing about 7 feet tall.
On July 11, 1972, two young boys were playing in their yard on the outskirts of Louisiana, Missouri.

Its name means 'little monk' in Neapolitan; it is often described as a 'benevolent man, short, stocky, very spiteful' who likes visiting houses in Naples' historic centre, wearing a long robe with a broad hood.

According to many tales he was the keeper (pozzari) of the city's underground aqueducts, canals and wells, who knew every passage and used the wells to slip secretly into the squares and homes of Naples.

For all his mischief, such as stealing valuables and bothering housewives, Monaciello is mostly benevolent: he appears at night to people in desperate need and leads them to hidden treasure or gives them his own valuables, asking nothing in return.
There is a saying for unexpected fortune: 'Forse avrà il Monaciello in casa' (perhaps he has had the little monk in his house).
Monaciello's habits resemble those of the water carriers of old Naples who worked in the tunnels linking the city's underground wells.
The French article calls Monaciello (O'Munaciello in Neapolitan), 'the little monk', a dwarf of Neapolitan folklore.

According to the first hypothesis, reported among others by Matilde Serao in her Leggende napoletane (1881), the munaciello was a real person whose story goes back to 1445, in the reign of Alfonso V of Aragon.
In that story the mother dressed her small, deformed child in a black-and-white monk's habit, hoping for a miracle, which gave rise to the people's nickname munaciello.
A red hood on his habit was taken as a good omen, while a black hood was linked to bad luck.
Another legend makes the munaciello the old keeper of the water wells (pozzaro), who, being small, could enter houses through the shafts used to lower the bucket.
A third hypothesis describes the munaciello as a little demon, spiteful because wicked, even when he leaves coins.
His presence must never be revealed: in Neapolitan folklore, misfortune can befall whoever tells of a visit from the munaciello.
Moñái is the third son of Tau and Kerana, one of the seven legendary monsters of Guarani mythology.
Because he dominates birds with his hypnotic antennae, he is called "the lord of the air".
Moñái likes to steal and hide his loot in a cave.
The Mongolian death worm is a creature alleged to live in the Gobi Desert.
Tales of it first reached the West through Roy Chapman Andrews's 1926 book On the Trail of Ancient Man.
In that book Andrews quotes Mongolian prime minister Damdinbazar, who described the worm in 1922.
It is shaped like a sausage about two feet long, with no head or legs, and so poisonous that touching it means instant death.
Andrews himself did not believe the creature existed.
In 1983 a Tartar sand boa was shown to locals who said they had seen the olgoi-khorkhoi, and they confirmed it was the same animal.
The worm is described as fat and bright red, 0.6 to 1.5 metres long.
Local Mongols claim the worm can spray acid and give off deadly electric shocks.
Because it resembles a cow's intestine, locals call it olgoi-khorkhoi, "intestine worm".

verified_claims.statement: The Mono Grande is a large monkey-like creature occasionally reported in South America.
Such creatures are reported as much larger than the known New World monkeys.
These accounts received little publicity and generally little or no interest from experts.

In the early 19th century, the German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt heard stories from the Orinoco about furry human-like creatures called Salvaje, rumoured to capture women, build huts and occasionally eat human flesh.
De Loys's ape, photographed by the Swiss geologist Francois de Loys in 1920 and proposed as an unknown great ape, was later identified as almost certainly a spider monkey.
Humboldt considered the Salvaje reports to be myths brought to South America by European colonists.
The Swedish author Rolf Blomberg (1966) speculated that rumours of hidden monsters in the Amazon basin may have been inspired by Arthur Conan Doyle's The Lost World (1912).
The term is sometimes used for yōkai or transformed beings.
Mononoke often appear in Heian literature.
The Aoi chapter of The Tale of Genji links Lady Rokujō’s living spirit with Aoi no Ue’s possession.
Ōkagami and Masukagami also mention mononoke.
The Pillow Book and Lady Murasaki’s diary record practices concerning mononoke.
Monopods were mythological dwarf-like creatures with a single large foot on a central leg.
Monopods appear in Aristophanes' The Birds, first staged in 414 BC.
Pliny the Elder describes them in his Natural History from travelers' tales of Monopods in India.
According to the Muisca, the monster inhabits Lake Tota in present-day Colombia.
The conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada described it as "A fish with a black head like an ox and larger than a whale".
A reported sighting took place in 1652.
The Monster of Ravenna was a possibly apocryphal monstrous birth of the late Renaissance whose appearance near Ravenna in early 1512 was widely reported in European pamphlets and diaries of the time.

Its grotesque features were read symbolically by opponents of both the Catholic Church and the Protestant Reformation, though the commoner explanation then was that it was an omen of the Battle of Ravenna (1512).
Modern medical consensus identifies the monster as a child with a severe congenital disorder.

According to the diary of Sebastiano di Branca Tedallini, the child was said to be born of a nun and a friar, with a horned head, the letters YXV on its chest, one hairy cloven-hoofed leg and a human eye in the middle of the other.
Luca Landucci described a single horn, bat wings, hermaphrodite genitals, an eye on the right knee and a clawed left foot like an eagle's.
In medieval Europe malformed infants with little chance of survival were commonly left to starve, and in Ravenna this was done on the Pope's order.
The signs on its chest were read as an upsilon (Υ), the desire for virtue, and a cross below it, Christ's teaching, which the Italians failed to follow.
The Macedonian article likewise says modern medical consensus identifies it as a child with severe congenital disorders.

The Moon Lake Monster, colloquially known as Moonie, is a cryptid reported to inhabit Moon Lake in Utah.
The creature legend has roots in folklore of the Ute people who avoided the area, describing it as inhabited by water spirits.
In East Asian mythology, the rabbit is seen as pounding with a mortar and pestle, but the contents of the mortar differ among Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese folklore.
In some Chinese versions, the rabbit pounds medicine for the mortals and some include making of mooncakes.
Touched by the rabbit's virtue, he drew the likeness of the rabbit on the Moon for all to see.
Moon folklore from certain Amerindian cultures of North America also has rabbit themes and characters.
Morag (lake monster) is documented as morag creature information in regional lore.
Mormo was a female spirit of Greek folklore whose name mothers and nurses invoked to scare children into behaving.
The plural mormones means "fearful ones" and relates to words meaning "fright".
Moroi is documented as moroi often associated in regional lore.
Morvarc'h is documented as morvarc breton horse in regional lore.
Moryana is documented as moryana russian pronounced in regional lore.
The concept is traced to nature spirits in China.
The Huainanzi describes a childlike form with dark red coloring.
Moss people is documented as moss both male in regional lore.
Despite its name, original sightings of the creature described avian, not lepidopteran, features.
The national press soon picked up reports and helped spread the story across the United States.
Mótsognir is documented as norse mythology norse in regional lore.
In Portuguese, Galician and Asturian mythology, the Mouros or Moiros are a race of supernatural beings who have lived in Galicia, Asturias and Portugal since the beginning of time.
For unknown reasons they had to take refuge underground and are now usually seen around castros and long barrows; they work gold, silver and gems into huge treasures guarded by cuélebres.
The Mouros rarely leave their dwellings except to get food and at special times such as Midsummer.
Galician anthropologists theorised that the Mouros are the opposite of the traditional Galician peasant.
The philologist Isodoro Millán derives the word from Celtic mrvos, akin to Indo-European mr-tuos and Latin mortuus, linking the Mouros to races already extinct or dead.
The Mouros encantados sometimes appear as giants or warriors, and include the legend of the moura encantada and the mourinhos or maruxinhos, a very small elf-like people.
According to the Spanish article, others link the name to Galician ouro, 'gold', since the Mouros lived in underground lairs and tunnels mining gold.
The male mouros were goldsmiths and sometimes dark-skinned as if foreign, while the female mouras were reputed sorceresses with red hair.
They trade with humans and pay in gold, but if the person tells others where the wealth came from, the gold turns to stones or coal.
The Russian article also calls the Mouros a race of supernatural beings inhabiting Galicia, Asturias and Portugal since the beginning of time.
Moussa Gname is a culture hero in epic tales of the Songhai in West Africa.
He is born of a woman impregnated by a spirit that dwells in a tree.
The boy is named for Moses because his father is not known.
His mother sent him to the tree where his spirit-father taught him hunting magic.
His greatest heroic feat was defeating the mythical monster the Hira.
This epic tradition was analyzed in Stephen Belcher's scholarly work Epic Traditions of Africa.

Mrenh kongveal (ម្រេញគង្វាល) are beings of Cambodian folk mythology like Western elves, associated with guarding animals; their roots seem uniquely Khmer; child-sized and mischievous, they are often given offerings when asked for help.
The Khmer word mrenh is fishermen's slang for 'one who catches fish' or, from Sanskrit, 'cancer'; kongveal means 'herdsman', 'guardian' or 'keeper'.
Originally they were seen as nomadic jungle beings herding wild herd animals like elephants; hunters, farmers and mahouts made offering baskets for them.

Today mrenh kongveal are supernatural guardians of a person, place or institution, protecting and guiding via whispers or dreams; unseen by adults, they can appear to pure-hearted children aged 6–14, and many in Cambodia claim to have seen them.
Muc-sheilche is documented as sheilche creature information in regional lore.
His narrative recounts heavy rain and dark skies for seven days.
He emerges from beneath the earth and shields Buddha with his hood.
The Mucalinda Sutta depicts the naga coiling around Buddha seven times.
After the sky clears he becomes a youth and bows before Buddha.
The Udana 2.1 translation says the naga king Muccalinda coils around Buddha seven times and spreads his hood.
Muckie is documented as irish folklore muckie in regional lore.
La Muelona ("big molar woman"), also Colmillona ("big fang woman"), is a figure of Colombian mythology from the Andean region (Huila and Tolima).
She appears at the path's edge as a seductive woman and crushes walkers with her teeth once in her arms.
The Mugwump is a lake monster which has been alleged to live in Lake Timiskaming, on the border of the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
The name mugwump comes from an Algonquin word.
The muki is a goblin-like creature of Central Andean mythology in Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.
He is a miner whose existence is confined underground: the muki lives inside the mines.
The muki is considered a dwarf, no taller than 2 feet.
In some mining traditions he has two horns to break rocks and point to mineral veins.
Sometimes he turns into an animal or a blond white man to deceive the miners.
Elders advise fighting the muki with one's belt without giving in to fear.

In Catalan mythology the Muladona or Donamula ('mule-woman') is a female mule with a woman's head; by legend a young woman cursed by her townsfolk for being irreverent and irreligious was turned into a mule.
She roamed the mountains, especially at night, joining mule trains, whose mules were so frightened they stampeded into ravines and died.
The Muladona looks like a mule but is a mix of human and animal: her mane is like a woman's hair, and her face, though animal-like, is clearly human.
She is always shown with a mule's four legs, sometimes with the front legs joined to a chest where a mule's neck would be, and always with breasts to stress she is female.
Muleteers fed their mules little Muladona-shaped breads so the animals would not take fright and would ignore her if she appeared.
According to the Spanish article, during the journey they kept counting their animals so the Muladona would not slip in among them unnoticed.
The Assamese article also calls the Muladona a female mule with a woman's head in Catalan mythology.
The Muldjewangk or Mulyawonk is a water creature in Ngarrindjeri mythology inhabiting the Murray River.
It was used as a deterrent for Aboriginal children wishing to play near the riverside after dark.
A legend tells of a Muldjewangk attacking a steamboat with two great hands grasping the hull.
The captain broke out in weeping red blisters over his body and took six months to die.
Large clumps of floating seaweed are said to hide Muldjewangks and are to be avoided.
The mullo (Muli for a female, Mulo for a male) is an undead, revenant or vampire of Roma folklore; the name means 'one who is dead'.
A mullo arises when someone dies suddenly of an unnatural cause or does not receive proper funeral rites.
A mullo is described with white clothes, hair to its feet and one physical oddity that varies by region; it seeks out and harasses people it disliked in life.

Mullos are believed to return to do harm or attack by strangling and sucking blood, usually from a relative who caused their death, neglected the burial rites, or kept the dead person's belongings instead of destroying them.
To get rid of a vampire, people hired a Dhampir, the son of a vampire and his widow, to detect it.
To ward off vampires, Romani people drove steel or iron needles into a corpse's heart and put bits of steel in the mouth, over the eyes and ears and between the fingers at burial.
They also put hawthorn in the corpse's sock or drove a hawthorn stake through the legs; other measures were staking the grave, pouring boiling water on it, beheading the corpse or burning it.

The Serbian article says the mullo is believed able to be invisible, look wholly normal, lack fingers or have animal body parts; in India it is described with yellow or flaming hair, and in Sweden it can change shape.
One often-mentioned trait is an insatiable sexual desire, which is why it is believed always to return to its partner.

The Muroni (or Murony) is a vampire of Wallachian mythology able to transform into various animals, so its attacks were hard to identify and often taken for animal attacks; the only sign of its presence was an exceptional loss of blood.
The Muroni is one of many vampire legends believed to be really a blood-sucking ghost, taking other forms only to make feeding easier.

Murony or muroni are old English corruptions of the Romanian term moroi, close to but distinct from the strigoi: it is mortal while the strigoi is immortal, but if a moroi is killed by a strigoi it becomes an immortal strigoi in turn.

Muu shuvuu is a mythological bird in Turkic and Mongolic mythology.

Tibetan and Himalayan art depicts nagas in serpent or partly human forms.

Naguals use their powers for good or evil according to their personality.
The general concept of nagualism is Mesoamerican in origin.
Nagualism is linked with pre-Columbian shamanistic practices through Pre-classic Olmec and Toltec depictions that are interpreted as human beings transforming themselves into animals.
Mesoamerican belief in tonalism, wherein every person has an animal counterpart to which their life force is linked, is drawn upon by nagualism.
Nahuelito is a lake monster said to live in Nahuel Huapi Lake, Patagonia, Argentina.
It has been described as a giant serpent, a huge hump or a plesiosaur.
The legend is believed to go back to indigenous stories from before the colonization of the Americas.
In 1897 Clemente Onelli, director of the Buenos Aires Zoo, began receiving reports of a strange creature in the Patagonian lakes.
George Garret's 1910 sighting was only made public in 1922, through the Toronto Globe newspaper.
In 1960 the Argentine Navy was said to have chased an unidentified underwater object in the lake for 18 days.
In 1988 photos of Nahuelito were published in a magazine of the Río Negro newspaper.
The Nain Rouge ("red dwarf") is a legendary creature of Detroit, Michigan, whose appearance presages misfortune for white settlers.
No records show the legend existed before the 1880s.
Detroit's founder Cadillac was told to appease the Nain Rouge but attacked it with his cane.

Namtar can be regarded as a minor god or a disease demon.
Namtar is known as Ereshkigal’s attendant deity.

verified_claims.statement: The Nandi bear is a cryptid purported to live in East Africa named from the Nandi people in western Kenya.
It is also known as Chemosit, Kerit, Koddoelo, Ngoloko, or Duba.
Descriptions note a ferocious powerfully built carnivore that is fierce, nocturnal, and can kill animals.
In 1914, Charles William Hobley authored a diagram of a footprint attributed to a Nandi bear.
Local legend holds the creature has reddish hair, long feet, and is said to scalp people.
The Nandi people call it kerit.
Nang mai is a young woman in a pleated robe with a sash and shoulder-length hair; the male version, rukkhadeva, inhabits banyans or large trees; villagers tie three-coloured cloth around her tree.
Thais believe good nang mai warn caring owners of danger, and evil ones lure men as husbands or kill them; Nang Tani and Nang Ta-khian are also nang mai.
Nang mai in large trees like the ta-khian are thought most hostile, since the bigger the tree the older and more haunting it is.

Nang Ta-khian is a nang mai tree spirit; oral tradition says she inhabits a ta-khian tree and sometimes appears as a beautiful young woman in reddish or brownish Thai dress, unlike the green-clad Nang Tani.
Nang Ta-khian, a forest spirit, haunts her tree's surroundings and houses with ta-khian beams, stilts or pillars; she may hurt the wicked who approach, but the righteous need not fear.
The ta-khian is almost never felled, for the spirit would be furious and follow the wood; it is used almost only in Buddhist monasteries, where monks' merit renders the spirit harmless.
Trees housing Ta-khian are traditionally wrapped in coloured satin, and monks wrap old trees to protect them from logging; felling requires a ceremony to ask permission.

In parts of Thailand, Nang Ta-khian has become a popular tree deity; miracles are credited to her, logs, beams or boat keels she is thought to inhabit are pilgrimage objects, and she is now often propitiated for lottery luck.
Larger shrines to Nang Ta-khian are in Sao Hai District, Saraburi, and Amphawa District, Samut Songkhram.
Nang Tani belongs to the tree-related female ghosts or fairies called nang mai; similar spirits exist in Cambodian and Lao tradition.
Nang Tani is also called Phi Tani ('Ghost of Tani') or Phrai Tani ('Nymph of Tani').
This ghost dwells in wild banana clumps and is pictured as a beautiful young woman in green Thai dress; she usually hides but comes out and is seen especially on full-moon nights.
Her skin is greenish, blending with the tree, her lips red like ripe ivy gourd, her hair black, thick and loose, and her feet hover slightly above the ground.
Cutting trees from Tani's clump is a bad omen; people offer sweets, incense and flowers, and tie coloured satin around the trunk.
Because of the ghostly link, people avoid growing it near homes; clumps are often at village outskirts or at the edge of fields by the road.
Thai oral legend says this spirit may harm men, especially those who wronged women, but she is mostly seen as benevolent and may give food to passing monks.
Amulets featuring Nang Tani are popular and come in many shapes and sizes.
Bashōnosei, Japanese ghostly banana trees, are listed as a similar ghost; they usually appear as a human face among banana leaves.
A Nargun was a fierce half-human half-stone creature living in the Den of Nargun in Victoria, Australia.
Aboriginal legend describes the Nargun as entirely made of stone except hands, arms and breast.
The creature dragged unwary travellers into its den and weapons turned back on their owner.

Nargun could not be harmed with boomerangs or spears as they reflected back.

Its name also refers to divination through the sound of a heated pot.

Nat worship predates Buddhism in Burma; after Buddhism arrived, the nats were syncretically merged with it.
Anawrahta used traditional nat spirits to attract people to his new religion.
Burma's most important nat pilgrimage site is Mount Popa, a 1,300-metre extinct volcano near Bagan.
Nats are given human characteristics, wants and needs, including desires considered immoral in mainstream Buddhism.
At a nat pwè, a festival to propitiate nats, nat kadaws (spirit mediums) dance and embody the nats.
Taungbyone north of Mandalay is a major nat festival site each Wagaung; Yadanagu at Amarapura is held a week later in honour of Popa Medaw.
Nat kadaws emerged as an independent profession in the latter half of the 19th century, and nat kannahs are more an urban phenomenon for migrants from the countryside.
Academic opinions differ on whether Burmese Buddhism and spirit worship are separate or a single religion.

The 37 Great Nats, recognized since the 11th century, were once high-status humans; all but Thagyamin died violently or painfully, e.g. snake bites, leprosy, beheading, immolation, drowning or falling off a swing.
Pilgrims climb Taung Kalat's 777 stairs to leave offerings at its summit shrines; money is standard, but other items suit the nat, such as whisky for Min Kyawzwa.
There are guardian spirits of trees, mountains, land, houses, villages, towns, the country and roads; some overlap, e.g. Min Mahagiri, leader of the 37 and protector of the household.
Throughout Myanmar there are hundreds of different nats supplicated through local and regional ceremonies (pwe).
The number 37 is a mystical ordering, said to come from Hindu cosmology, used often in Burmese history since the Bagan period.
The formalizing of the 37 Great Nats by King Anawrahta (1044–1077) of Bagan has been interpreted as Burmanisation and the establishment of Bamar supremacy in the Irrawaddy valley.
Nats who are deceased humans still in limbo between lives are called nat sein, those who died a violent death; they make up most of the 37.
He is a common motif in Odisha's Pattachitra art.

Nuberu, Nubero (Castilian) or Nubeiro (Galician), literally 'The Clouder', is a figure of Asturian, Cantabrian, Galician and Leonese mythology.
In Asturian mythology the Nuberu (in western Asturias also Reñubeiru or Xuan Cabritu) is the god of clouds and storms.
In some stories he is one being, in others a species of dwarf-like weather-controlling beings, and sometimes a thick-bearded man in goatskins and a big hat.
As a single being, Nuberu wears dark pelts, rides a wolf-drawn chariot and wears a patch over an injured or missing eye.
He can be terribly cruel, damaging fields and pastures, but kind to those who once helped him, and by myth he lives in the city of Orito in Egypt.
Folklorists see Nuberu as an Asturian remnant of the ancient sky god Taranis, worshipped in Asturias until the Middle Ages.
Its closest Spanish parallel is the Entiznáu of Extremadura, an evil weather creature of similar look and dress but different size.
Nuberu once fell from a cloud and only one peasant would shelter him; in thanks, Nuberu watered his fields, gave him good harvests and still brings rain to the region.
Years later the peasant, in Egypt, heard his wife was to remarry; he asked Nuberu for help, and they rode the clouds back to Asturias in time to stop the wedding.
Fishermen fear the Nuberu, blaming him for the strong north-westerly winds of the Cantabrian Sea that drive them hurriedly back to port.
In Cantabrian mythology the Nuberus are often many little creatures, small, chubby and mischievous, with devilish grins and little black wings.
In southern Galicia Nubeiros are small hairy men with long twisted tails who fly on grey clouds and cause dry summer storms and lightning.
Elsewhere in Galicia, Nuberu forges lightning himself in his mountain ironworks, then rides the sky to cause storms and hurl his creations.

The nuno sa punso ('old man of the mound'), or nuno ('old man', 'ancestor'), is a dwarf-like nature spirit of Philippine mythology believed to live in an anthill or termite mound.
The nuno are ancestral spirits; before felling a tree or breaking new ground, people ask their permission to avoid the misfortune of angering them.

The nuno is a tiny old man, unlike the playful dwende who appears to children; the nuno is easily angered and punishes those who damage his mound, e.g. swelling the foot that kicked it; he also lives under large rocks, trees, riverbanks, caves or gardens.
Nunos can curse trespassers with swelling or pain and excessive back hair, usually by spitting on them.

It is commonly believed in the Philippines that illness modern medicine cannot cure may be a nuno's curse; the victim goes to an albularyo, a traditional healer, who performs pagtatawas divination with alum or wax melted into water.
To be cured, the victim's family may offer fruit, food, drink or an object to the nuno; if still ill, they may need to ask its forgiveness in person.
Elders in the Philippine provinces taught people always to excuse themselves (tabi tabi po) when passing an earth mound.

Nymphs are minor female nature deities or spirits in Greek myth.
Nymphs are depicted as young women with attributes of their habitats.

Ancient Greek nymph types were fluid rather than rigid categories.
Naiads are freshwater nymphs of springs, rivers, streams, wells, and fountains.

The word ogre is French, from the Etruscan god Orcus, first attested in Chrétien de Troyes's late 12th-century romance Perceval, li contes del graal.

This wild, fierce and vengeful creature lives in deep, gloomy caves in the remotest parts of La Montaña, their entrances blocked with brush and boulders.
