Orang bunian are beautiful, in ancient Southeast Asian dress, nearly identical to humans, some lacking a philtrum; modern depictions add elf-like features, pointed ears, fantasy attire or Minangkabau long coats.
Orang bunian are said to live in deep forests or high mountains of Sumatra, Borneo and the Malay Peninsula, also near settlements, even sharing houses with human families.
By legend their society resembles the ancient Malay Peninsula, with families, clans and royalty; they have supernatural powers and must be appeased with rituals before humans enter their land.
Orang bunian are generally benevolent, befriending and helping humans, especially dukun, bomoh and pawang; they can marry humans and bear invisible children.
Men who returned from bunian society found many years had passed and everyone they knew had died; these tales are compared to Urashima Taro and Rip Van Winkle.
Even non-believers often come to see the forest not as empty space but as somewhere deserving humility.
These narratives are compared to Urashima Taro and Rip Van Winkle.
In Malay folklore, the Orang Mawas or Mawas (also Orang Dalam) is a cryptid reported in the jungles of Johor (Malaysia) and Singapore.
The mawas is described as about 2.4–3 m tall, bipedal and black-furred, reportedly eating fish and raiding orchards.
The local Orang Asli call it hantu jarang gigi ('snaggle-toothed ghost'); recorded mawas sighting claims date back to 1871.
Some speculate it is a surviving Gigantopithecus or folk memory of one, while scientists tend to dismiss sightings as misidentified sun bears.
In Sumatra, mawas (sometimes maias) is a common name for the orangutan.

In Malay ghost belief, the Orang Minyak ('oily man') is a supernatural being coated in shiny black grease who abducts young women at night; the legend is first mentioned in a Berita Harian (Singapore) report of 12 October 1957.
It supposedly climbs walls and grabs victims while escaping thanks to its slippery coating, first described as hair oil, later coconut oil and soot; films show it in crude oil.
Many stories call it a rapist targeting only virgins; from the 1950s it was blamed for rapes, and superstitious Malay female students wore sweaty clothing to ward it off.
Some versions hold the Orang Minyak is an evil human warlock, not a supernatural being.
Science writer Benjamin Radford called the tales rooted in myth and folklore and the creature's abilities implausible.
Singaporean writer Yogesh Tulsi says the crude-oil Orang Minyak represents traditional life ruined by petro-modernity.
In Indonesian folklore, Orang Pendek (Indonesian for 'short person') is the most common name for a creature said to inhabit remote mountain forests on the island of Sumatra.
Witnesses agree the primate is a ground-dwelling, bipedal ape with short fur, 80–150 cm tall.
Claimed sightings have occurred mostly in Kerinci Regency, central Sumatra, especially within Kerinci Seblat National Park.
According to Suku Anak Dalam legends, Orang Pendek has for centuries been part of their world and a co-inhabitant of the forest.
The Suku Anak Dalam are nomadic groups who have traditionally lived in the lowland forests of Jambi and South Sumatra.
The Orang Rimba of Bukit Duabelas speak of the Hantu Pendek, closely matching Orang Pendek but seen as a supernatural entity or demon rather than an animal; the name means 'short ghost'.
According to the Orang Rimba, the Hantu Pendek travel in groups of five or six, live on wild yams, hunt with small axes, and ambush hunters traveling alone in the forest.
Along the Makekal River, people tell a legend of their ancestors outsmarting these cunning but dim-witted creatures while hunting; the story is used to boast of their intellect.
Dutch settlers in the early 20th century introduced Westerners to Orang Pendek-like animals in Sumatra.

Van Heerwarden wrote that the creature's face was neither repulsive nor ugly, nor at all apelike.

Local folklore also has the cigau and the orang gadang, a kind of local bigfoot.

verified_claims.statement: In Finnish mythology Otso (also Karhu, Ohto, Kontio, Metsän kuningas and Mesikämmen) is a bear, the sacred king of animals and leader of the forest, deeply feared and respected by old Finnish tribes, and he appears in the national epic Kalevala.
Otso is not a particular bear's spirit but the collective animistic spirit of all bears.
Some stories tell that Ukko, the weather god, threw wool into the sea and Otso was born from the bits of wool that reached the shore; others say Otso was born from the Ursa Major constellation.

The oldest myths about Otso tell of his marriage to the primordial mother of all people, reflected in the Peijaiset ritual, in which the bear spirit was symbolically returned to its family through marriage.
If the ancient Finns had to kill a bear, a sacred Peijaiset ritual was held, in which the bear's skull was mounted on a pine tree.

Otso ("broad forehead"), Ohto, Kontio, metsän kuningas ("king of the forest") and mesikämmen ("honey paw") are the main circumlocutions in Finnish mythology for the spirit of the bear, which must never be named.
The sacred songs of the bear cult concern most peoples of Finno-Ugric tradition: Finns, Estonians, Sami, Mordvins, Khanty and Mansi.

Papa Bois or Papa Bwa (also called Maître Bois and Daddy Bouchon), from a French patois word meaning "father of the forest", is a folklore character of St. Lucia, Dominica, Grenada and Trinidad and Tobago.

verified_claims.statement: Pard (Ancient Greek πάρδος) is the Ancient Greek word for the leopard, listed in medieval bestiaries and in Pliny the Elder's Natural History.
Pliny writes that cheetahs were believed to be hybrids born of a promiscuous lioness and the pard.
Pliny also says the passion between pard and lioness is so violent that it enrages the male lion, who takes revenge on the lioness when he smells the pard on her.
In the 7th-century Etymologies, Isidore of Seville describes their coats as mottled like a giraffe's and calls them 'headlong for blood', able to kill prey in one leap.

Only in the 13th century did pards gain their mythic reputation as bloodthirsty, almost demonic creatures, chiefly through the MS Bodley 764 Bestiary, in which their spots symbolised sins, the devil or the many vices of mankind.
The pardus is an animal of medieval bestiaries, a spotted, extremely fast feline believed to mate with lions to produce leopards.
Pari, or peri, is a supernatural being originating in Persian tales and spreading through Asian folklore.

Paris are said to abduct people and take them to Paristan.

The Patagons or Patagonian giants were a mythical race of giant humans said in early European accounts to live in Patagonia.
They were said to be at least twice normal human height, some accounts giving 13 to 15 feet.
Tales of them shaped European ideas of the region for nearly 300 years.
The first mention came from Ferdinand Magellan and his crew, who claimed to see them while sailing the South American coast during their 1520s circumnavigation.
The voyage account says a naked man of giant stature was seen on the shore, dancing, singing and throwing dust on his head.
He was so tall that the sailors reached only to his waist.
Pigafetta recorded that Magellan gave these people the name Patagão.
The Patagon story was believed for 250 years until it was disproved in the late 18th century.
The place name Patagonia comes from the meaning "land where the Patagons live".
The Patasola, or "single leg", is a Colombian folk legend of a female jungle monster who appears to hunters or loggers in the wilderness when they think about women.
The Patasola appears as a beautiful, seductive woman, often like a loved one, and lures a man away from his companions into the jungle.
There it reveals its true, hideous form: a one-legged creature with a vampire-like lust for human flesh and blood.
Popular belief places it in mountain ranges, virgin forests and other densely wooded areas.
The Patasola is usually seen as a protector of nature and forest animals, unforgiving toward people who enter to damage them.
Her single leg ends in a cloven, cow-like hoof.
She is also believed to turn into other animals, such as a large black dog or a cow.
Some believe she was a mother who killed her own son and was banished to the woods as punishment.
Others say she was a cruel temptress whose leg was chopped off with an axe and thrown into a fire.
According to legend, she is the tormented soul of an unfaithful woman who dishonoured her husband.
They are nocturnal or active on foggy days as direct sunlight can be fatal.
They prefer raw food and have an aversion to steam and fire.
Patupaiarehe live in deep forests and mountainous regions, hostile to human intruders.

His tall tales revolve around his superhuman labors, and he is customarily accompanied by Babe the Blue Ox (French: Babe le bœuf bleu ), his pet and working animal.

Several researchers have attempted to trace Paul Bunyan to the character of Bon Jean of French Canadian folklore.
Some of these stories include motifs from older folktales, such as absurdly severe weather and fearsome critters.

Pazuzu amulets are placed in dwellings to protect infants from Lamashtu.

Pé de garrafa ("bottle foot") is a legendary creature of Brazilian folklore, named for its rounded foot like the bottom of a bottle, which leaves strange round footprints.
It is said to live in the forest and to be quite tall.
The creature makes shrill calls in the forest that make hunters think it is a lost companion.
Following the call confuses the pursuer further, as the sound bounces, amplifies and can cause delirium and madness.
The creature is blamed for witchcraft, but it is unclear whether it is a man-eater.
The Pé de garrafa was first described by Alfredo do Vale Cabral (1884) as a local legend of the state of Piauí.
It is also known as the monster leaving huge footprints in the sandy and clayey soil of Massapê, Ceará, in northeastern Brazil.
Cascudo wrote that it is a variant of the Mapinguari and Capelobo legends, though there is no testimony that it is a man-eater like them.
Gustavo Barroso called it a "species of Caapora" (Caipora), while Vale Cabral (1884) only said it shared the Caapora's forest habitat.
Pearlin Jean is documented as pearlin jean given in regional lore.
Pebet is a bird of Meitei mythology and folklore in Kangleipak, said to be smaller than a sparrow.
Mother pebet teaches the chicks to fly to make them safer from the cat.
When the cat attacks, the mother tells the chicks to fly, but the youngest is caught.
The Peluda (Spanish) or La Velue ('The Hairy One', originally French) is a mythical beast that terrorised the River Huisne area of France in the Middle Ages.
This serpent-headed creature had a body of long green fur with poison-tipped spines; it caused floods (or spat fire) that ruined crops, ate livestock and people, and killed with its tail.
It was defeated after trying to prey on a maiden named l'Agnelle; her fiancé killed it with a sword-stroke to the tail, its only weak spot.
A pamphlet on 'La Velue' was printed in 1889 for the Sarthe area, its text also describing the beast.
French sources say the beast was serpent-headed and serpent-tailed, ox-sized, with an egg-shaped body covered in 'long green fur'.
Cordonnier-Détrie held that the beast belonged to the same family as the Tarasque of Tarascon and Beaucaire.
According to the lore, the beast was refused a place on Noah's Ark yet survived the Flood.
By popular tradition it died at the bridge of Yvré-l'Évêque; the victory was long celebrated at La Ferté-Bernard and Connerré, and its body was reportedly stuffed.
The Indonesian article says its name comes from Occitan for 'hairy', its body is like a porcupine's, and it is ox-sized.
The Japanese article calls the peluda or velue, 'the shaggy one', a monster told of in the Sarthe department of northern France.

verified_claims.statement: The penanggalan or penanggal is a nocturnal vampiric being of Malay ghost lore, a floating woman's head with organs and entrails trailing from the neck; from afar it twinkles like a ball of flame.
The name penanggalan derives from tanggal, meaning to remove or take off.
The penanggalan is a witch who gained that form through meditation in a vinegar vat, and by day is a living human.
In Malaysian folklore, penanggal are mortal women practising black magic; to become one, a woman meditates in a vinegar bath with all but her head submerged.
The penanggal is also mentioned in the Hikayat Abdullah, written in 1845.
Those whose blood the penanggalan drinks contract an almost always fatal wasting disease, and anyone brushed by its dripping entrails suffers painful open sores.
As traditional Malay houses stood on stilts, the penanggal hid beneath them and lapped up a new mother's blood with its long tongue.
The most common protection is scattering the thorny leaves of the mengkuang plant.
Singapore penanggalan stories date back to 1912 but have probably existed longer.
As an extra precaution, a pregnant woman can keep scissors or betel cutters under her pillow, as the penanggalan fears them.
The Manananggal of the Philippines belongs to the same group.
The penanggalan belongs to a group of similar mythological beings known by different names across Southeast Asia.
The Pend Oreille Paddler is a cryptid which inhabits Lake Pend Oreille in North Idaho.
The monster's first appearance in the North Idaho lake was reported in 1944.
Penghou is a tree spirit in Chinese lore.
Two early Chinese writings preserve related accounts of it.
One text describes it as arising from the essence of wood.
The same tradition gives it the shape of a black dog without a tail.
Pereplut is documented as pereplut slavic deity in regional lore.
The Pesanta is like the Portuguese Pisadeira; it is black and hairy, with steel paws that have holes in them.
Its holed paws mean it cannot pick anything up from the ground without dropping it.
As soon as someone wakes, it runs off through the smallest gap in the window or the keyhole, and one only glimpses a small fleeing shadow.
By day the Pesanta is said to hide in churches or abandoned houses, and in the Garrotxa people believe it hides in volcanic craters.
The figure of the Pesanta is linked to a parasomnia called sleep paralysis.
The Spanish article calls it a mythological animal shaped like a huge dog, rarely a cat.
The tiny spirit, perhaps only a few feet tall, is often described carrying many keys and roaming the vaults and tunnels under the castle, unlocking doors as he goes.
He is also the keeper and watchman of the castle, rewarding the honest and good while punishing or driving away thieves and intruders.
Petermännchen is also said to have woken soldiers who fell asleep on night watch to save them from punishment.

Legend says that when Christianity reached Schwerin, a pagan god worshipped where the castle now stands fled, leaving his spirit servants; all of them eventually left except Petermännchen, who would not abandon his post.

Petermännchen is said to have tormented Wallenstein, granted the Duchy of Mecklenburg by Emperor Ferdinand II in 1628, so badly on his first night at Schwerin Palace that the general left the next morning utterly sleepless.
Richard Wossidlo interpreted some legends as making Petermännchen the god Radegast turned into a kobold, left behind to guard the sacred treasure of the Obotrites.
Petitcrieu (also Petitcreiu, Petitcru or Pticru) is a legendary magical dog of Arthurian legend, found in the chivalric romance of Tristan and Iseult.
In Gottfried von Strassburg's Tristan, Petitcrieu was a magical fairy dog from Avalon owned by Duke Gilan of Wales, a goddess's love token.
Petitcrieu was indescribably beautiful and many-coloured, with a magic golden bell on its collar whose sweet ring made anyone who heard it happy.
It also had no appetite and could not eat.
Tristan struck a deal with the Duke to kill the giant Urgan for the dog.
The Phantome, known in Guyana as the Moongazer, is a figure in the folklore of Saint Lucia, Trinidad and Tobago and Guyana.
It is described as an extremely tall spectre standing at crossroads on full-moon nights, legs straddling the road.
Anyone who passes beneath it and interrupts its moongazing is crushed when it snaps its legs shut.
The only warning is a shrill whistle just before the attack.
The Phantome can make itself invisible; only its shadow in the moonlight reveals it.
In some versions, a traveller who quietly walks around it is unharmed, but one who taunts it or distracts its gaze from the moon has their brain consumed through its palm.
Per the Royal Institute Dictionary 1999, tai hong means to die an unnatural, violent death, such as murder or drowning.
These ghosts symbolize how life can end unpredictably; suicides and executed prisoners are excluded because their deaths were anticipated.
The first seven days after death are when the spirit most seeks revenge; Phi Tai Hong often try to kill others the way they died, making them among the most feared ghosts.
They are hard to exorcise because they are so violent and haunt their death place, including houses.
Tai Thang Klom are ghosts of pregnant women who died with their unborn child, more malevolent for having the power of two spirits.
According to Jeremias van Vliet, a Dutch East India Company director in 17th-century Ayutthaya, pregnant women buried alive under fortifications became protective spirits.
The condition comes from raising the glowing white-leaved magical plant wan phi phong; as it matures its leaves resemble the grower's face, who eventually becomes Phi Phong.
By day Phi Phong looks ordinary; by night a soft flame glows in its nose; like the krasue, krahang and pop it eats frogs, dung, corpses and afterbirth and avoids humans.
Phi Phong usually harms no one unless provoked; angered, it throws objects onto the roof, and illness, misfortune and death then plague the household.
One way to destroy a Phi Phong is to correctly name a person aloud as one; the curse also spreads through saliva.
Piasa is a later name for the creature(s) of Native American mythology shown in a mural painted high on cliffs above the Mississippi River.
Its original site was at the end of a chain of limestone bluffs in Madison County, at present-day Alton, Illinois.
French explorers Marquette and Louis Jolliet (1673) described the original paintings as a multicoloured human-faced creature with a long fish-finned tail.
A contemporary sketch shows a wingless, scaly four-legged beast identifiable as the underwater panther type.
Folklorists consider the legend of chieftain Ouatoga fighting the bird to be fakelore invented by John Russell (1836, 1848).
The wall bearing the original paintings at Alton was probably destroyed around the 1850s.
The mural was restored with replicas several times in the 20th century.
Another source calls the piasa a 19th-century invention passed off as a legendary creature of Native North American mythology.
The picolaton (also called pique-au-mollet, quiperlibresson and cacalambri) is an imaginary bird of the folklore of Franche-Comté.
It is best known as a creature used to threaten lazy children, who are told the picolaton will nip their heels and buttocks if they do not hurry; it is thus akin to the bogeyman.
Especially irritating children are promised a visit to the bird's incredible nest around April Fool's Day if they are very good; it supposedly nests in thorn bushes.
The Bengali article likewise calls the picolaton an imaginary bird of Franche-Comté folk belief.

The Pincoy is a male sea water spirit of Chilote mythology in Chiloé, Chile.
He resembles a merman with a large golden sea-lion body, a handsome face and long golden hair, magically attractive to women.
He is the son of Millalobo, king of the seas, and the human Huenchula; his sisters are the Sirena chilota and the Pincoya, who is also his wife.
With his sisters he carries the dead from the sea to the Caleuche.
He sings a beautiful, strange song so the Pincoya begins her magical dance for the fertility of the sea.
In local mythology, the Pincoya is a female water spirit of the Chilotan seas.
The Pincoya has long blond hair and incomparable beauty, is cheerful, and rises from the sea's depths.
She personifies the fertility of marine species.
If she dances facing the sea, fish will be plentiful; facing the mountains, seafood will be scarce.
Other legends make her the daughter of Millalobo, king of the sea, and the human Huenchula.
Her sister is the Sirena chilota and her brother Pincoy, who is also her husband.
The three siblings guide drowned sailors onto the phantom ship Caleuche.

The pishtaco is a folk bogeyman of the Andes, especially Peru and Bolivia, that extracts its victims' fat.
It is thought to stem from Spanish conquistadors using the corpse fat of Indigenous Peruvians to treat wounds and illnesses.
In the Bolivian Altiplano it has the Aymara names kharisiri ("slaughterer") or lik'ichiri ("fat-maker").
He is often pictured as a white or mestizo man armed with a long knife for beheading or dismembering victims.
The pishtaco may also leave no visible wound yet cause death after a few days.
In the Andean tradition of the Quechua and Aymara in Peru and Bolivia, it is a monstrous, usually white murderer who sucks the fat from the Indigenous people he kills.
Pitsen is a forest creature in the mythology of the Siberian Tatars.
Its role is contradictory: it can bring luck but also trouble, leading people into the wilderness.
Pitsen often changes shape, appearing as an old man with staff and knapsack or as animals such as apes; it likes derelict lodges, riding horses and smearing their manes with tar.
In one legend a hunter married a beautiful maiden met in the forest and grew rich, but coming home early he saw a tusked monster eating lizards; he cried out, and his wife and wealth vanished.
Pitsen is a counterpart of the Chuvash Arçuri and the Volga-Ural Tatar Şüräle.
In Siberian Tatar mythology Pitsen is the spirit-master of the forest.
Pitsen is also called bichen, pichan, pechan, pitsin, en, enperi or urman iyase.
The Piuchén is a vampiric creature of Mapuche and Chilote mythology known across much of Chile.
It often appears as a flying snake or a bat-winged lizard whose whistles or hisses stun or kill prey.
The lore may come from encounters with the common vampire bat.

verified_claims.statement: The Pombero is a mythological being typical of Paraguay's heritage.
It is a small humanoid creature of Guarani mythology.
He is also called Pyrague ("hairy feet"), Karai Pyhare ("lord of the night") and Kuarahy Jára ("master of the sun").
In the old legend, the servant who took the prince's body could not return to his destroyed body, so his spirit moves from body to body eating intestines.

Village legend says the ghost lives in a sorceress and leaves while she sleeps; before she dies it must find a new body, which receives it by swallowing her saliva; when it haunts someone, it eats their intestines as they sleep.
One rumoured way to get rid of a pop is to call a healing dancer who drives it out with a spinning dance.
Especially among the Isan, a pop is believed to take animal forms, most often a black dog; Thai folklore distinguishes ordinary, hereditary and face-switching pops, with Ha Gom as their lord.
In November 1892, under King Rama V, an incident in Uttaradit concerned an old Phuan man named Ta Puang, rumoured to be a pop after three young women died mysteriously.
The Pope Lick Monster is a legendary part-man, part-goat, part-sheep creature said to live under a railroad trestle over Pope Lick Creek in Louisville, Kentucky.
Some accounts say it uses hypnosis or voice mimicry to lure trespassers onto the trestle to die before an oncoming train.
Other stories say it jumps from the trestle onto the roofs of passing cars.
Other legends say it was a circus performer who vowed revenge after being mistreated.
The legends made the area a legend-tripping site, and there have been several deaths and accidents at the trestle since it was built.
In reality the bridge carries a major rail line into Louisville.

Poubi Lai is a dragon python of Meitei mythology and folklore dwelling in Manipur's Loktak Lake.

Preta is a supernatural being suffering extreme hunger and thirst in Asian religious traditions.
The term hungry ghost mainly fits East Asian adaptations; the early Petavatthu has more varied forms.

Preta traditions originate in Indian religions and spread to East Asia through Buddhism.
Preta in Sanskrit means a departed or deceased person.
In the Tirokudda Kanda, hungry shades live on gifts from the living.
A pricolici (same form in the plural) is a Romanian vampire with werewolf traits, arising from a child breastfed again after weaning.
Pricolici resemble the vârcolac, but always have wolf traits and can turn into ordinary people or animals.
Unlike the strigoi, which keeps a human look, the pricolici always resembles a wolf or dog; wicked, violent men are often said to become pricolici after death to keep harming people.
Some Romanian folklore holds that pricolici are werewolves in life and return as vampires after death.
Even in modern times many rural Romanians have claimed to be attacked by unusually large, fierce wolves that strike silently, suddenly and only lone victims.
The word's origin is unknown, though it may come from Latin lycus, 'wolf'.
The Spanish article also calls them werewolves in life who return as vampires, the root of the legend of vampires turning into wolves, dogs, owls or bats.
According to the Russian article, pricolici were the dead risen from the grave as wolves or dogs, and also living people able to turn into wolves or dogs for a time.
The Proctor Valley Monster is a cryptid said to live in Proctor Valley, California.
Sightings link it to the Proctor Valley Road, a dirt road connecting Jamul to the Eastlake neighborhood of Chula Vista.
Accounts vary, but the two most common versions are a tall, hairy Bigfoot type or a "disarranged cow" bovine type.
The nearby Bonita Museum & Cultural Center claims to display an unknown humanoid footprint that many locals see as evidence of the cryptid.

The pugot moves very fast, eats snakes and insects in trees by thrusting food into its neck stump, and is fairly harmless though frightening; it likes to take women's underwear from the clothesline.
The pugot appears in the Ifugao myth Tulud Nimputul: The Self-Beheaded, where the hero feeds it chopped chicken mixed with blood.
The Pukwudgie is a mischievous or menacing dwarfish human-like creature of Native American lore.

Qarakorshaq is an animal-like mythical creature in Turkic mythology.
It is said to hide in dark places, holes or empty houses to seize, carry off and devour its victim, but light and noise scare it away; it walks clumsily.
Analysis of its traits suggests it may come from folk memory of real animals long extinct in parts of Anatolia.
In Turkish it is called Karakorşak, an animal-like mythical creature of Turkic mythology.

Qareen is a human’s spiritual double, understood as part of the person or a complementary creature in a parallel realm.

Qiongqi is a mythological creature in Chinese classics counted among the Four Perils.

Qiulong is a Chinese dragon with conflicting definitions about the presence of horns.

The same characters are sometimes used in Japan for mizuchi, a river dragon.

The Queensland tiger is a creature in Australian folklore reputed to inhabit Queensland.
Known as yarri, it is described as a dog-sized striped feline with violent temperament.
It has been hypothesized as a survivor or descendant of the predatory marsupial Thylacoleo.
The 'bull with five horns' was likened by Pseudo-Fredegar, interpolating Gregory of Tours, to both Neptune and the Minotaur, being both seaborne and bull-like.

It is unknown whether the sea and bull traits are original or added by the Christian authors, and the clerical Latin name does not show whether it translates a genuine Frankish creature or is a coinage.
According to the French article, the name Quinotaurus means 'bull with five horns'.

The Rainbow Serpent is a common creator deity known by many names across Aboriginal languages.
The serpent is a widespread motif in Australian Aboriginal art and religion.
Numerous names and traditions communicate the sacred power of the serpent in The Dreaming.

In Cantabrian mythology the ramidreju is a creature said to live in the mountains and forests of Cantabria in northern Spain; this weasel-like animal is born once every hundred years from a weasel or a marten.
Its body is very long like a snake's, its fur greenish, its eyes yellow, its nose like a hog's and its tusks like a boar's, which it uses to dig very deep holes.
Ramidrejus are much sought after in Cantabrian folklore because their fur cures every illness and the animal has a strong craving for gold.
It was described by the Cantabrian scholar Manuel Llano, from an account he said he heard from a resident of Viaña (Cabuérniga).
Its bile, drunk by the anjanas in the Cieza valley, can cure all illnesses and reveal hidden treasures.
The Spanish article describes it as a hybrid of the monuca galana (weasel) and the rámila (stone marten), slender and long, with black-and-green striped skin, a boar's face and yellow eyes.
The Esperanto article also says ramidrejus are much sought because they help find hidden treasure and their fur reputedly cures every disease.
The child-eating Rangda leads evil witches against Barong, leader of the forces of good; their battle is shown in the Barong dance as the eternal struggle of good and evil.
Rangda is an Old Javanese term meaning widow.
Rangda is depicted as a mostly nude old woman with long unkempt hair, pendulous breasts and claws, with a fanged, goggle-eyed mask and long protruding tongue.
Rangda is known as a leyak queen, incarnation of Calon Arang, the legendary witch who wreaked havoc in ancient Java under Airlangga in the late 10th century.
Rangda is linked to the legend of Calon Arang and to that of Mahendradatta, a divorced and exiled Javanese queen.
Rangda's name means widow in Balinese and comes from the 12th-century Javanese-Balinese tale Calonarang.
Mahendradatta, from whom other interpretations derive Rangda, was wife of the Balinese king Udayana and Airlangga's mother, known for her devotion to Durga in Bali.
Calon Arang was a widow skilled in black magic who damaged crops and brought disease; her daughter Ratna Manggali could not find a husband because people feared her mother.
In Balinese Hinduism, Rangda is the supreme manifestation of the evil aspects of power.
In performance Rangda moves wildly like an animal with reckless gestures and a leaping gait.
As a manifestation of Durga, Rangda is consort of the god Siwa; her realm is the cemetery, and her sacred masks are kept in village temples of the dead.
In the battle reenacted at least once a year in Balinese villages, Rangda is defeated but never killed, since her negative energy coexists with the positive.
Research shows Rangda's role in Bali is more than an artistic device; she also serves a religious function as a sacred symbol.
Rwa Bhineda, a Balinese philosophy of balance between two opposing poles, is explicitly manifested in the relationship of Rangda and Barong.
The Lontar Siwa Tattwa and Lontar Usada Taru Premana identify Rangda as the goddess Durga on earth with the title Hyang Bherawi.
In Balinese Hinduism, the struggle to maintain or restore the cosmological balance of opposing forces, such as good and evil, permeates all of life.
King Airlangga asked his advisor Empu Bharada to deal with the problem; Empu Bharada sent his disciple Empu Bahula to marry Ratna.
Empu Bahula found Calon Arang's book and gave it to Empu Bharada; the angry Calon Arang fought Empu Bharada and, without Durga's help, was defeated.
The next day a great flood engulfed the village, many died, and disease appeared.
In tales she abducts men and takes them to her lair.

El Ratoncito Pérez or Ratón Pérez ('Pérez the Little Mouse') is a fantasy figure of early childhood in Spanish and Hispanic American cultures.

By tradition, children who lose a milk tooth put it under the pillow or on the bedside table, and he comes while they sleep and replaces it with a small payment or gift, like the Tooth Fairy elsewhere.
He first appeared in oral folktales such as The Vain Little Mouse, but it was Luis Coloma who in 1894 made him a tooth collector in a tale written for the eight-year-old King Alfonso XIII.

Queen Maria Christina commissioned the tale for Alfonso XIII, who had just lost a tooth; in Coloma's story Ratón Pérez lives with his family in a biscuit box in the basement of the Prast confectionery in Madrid.

He is usually called El Ratoncito Pérez, except in parts of Mexico, Guatemala, Peru and Chile, where he is El Ratón de los Dientes (the Tooth Mouse), and in Argentina, Venezuela, Uruguay and Colombia, where he is El Ratón Pérez.
According to the Spanish article, the most likely origin is the 18th-century French tale by Baroness d'Aulnoy, La Bonne Petite Souris.
Elsewhere other beings collect teeth, such as the Tooth Fairy in Germanic countries, l'Angelet or La rateta in Catalonia and Maritxu teilatukoa in the Basque Country.
The Russian article also says he gives a child a present in exchange for a milk tooth placed under the pillow.
Ravana is the rakshasa king of Lanka traditionally depicted with ten heads.
He abducts Sita and holds her in Ashoka Vatika.
Rama fights him with Sugriva and the vanara army's support and kills him.
His defeat is commemorated by burning Ravana effigies at Dussehra.
Ravana is regarded as a devotee of Shiva.
He also appears in the Lankavatara Sutra, Buddhist Jatakas, and Jain Ramayanas.
The name Ravana is explained as meaning roaring.
The epithet Dashanana means the one with ten heads.
His other names include Lankapati and Lankeshwara.
Brahma grants him immunity against his creations except humans in the story.
Brahma's gifts also include weapons, a chariot, and shapeshifting.
Mandodari, Maya's daughter, is described as his chief queen.
Mackenzie describes Rama as the slayer of Ravana who oppresses humans in the Ramayana.
The Carlos Museum collection scene depicts Ravana carrying Sita from her forest hermitage.
In Arizona folklore, the Red Ghost is a figure said to have roamed the Arizona frontier in the late 19th century.
It was said to be a large red camel with a bleached human skeleton on its back.
Background: War Secretary Jefferson Davis's proposal to use camels was approved in 1855 in what became the Camel Corps.
The legend began in 1883, when two men left their ranch house near Eagle Creek.
On returning, they found one wife trampled to death.
The Red Lady of Huntingdon College is a ghost said to haunt the former Pratt Hall dormitory at Huntingdon College in Montgomery, Alabama.

He and his sister Signý are the children of Völsung and his wife Hljod, and Sigmund is best known as the father of Sigurð the dragon-slayer.

The singa is an apotropaic figure of Batak mythology, North Sumatra, Indonesia, representing benevolent protective power; described as part human, part water buffalo and part crocodile or lizard, with an elongated face, bulging eyes, defined nose and long spiral beard; other figures sometimes stand on its head.

Singa comes from Sanskrit singa ('lion'); in Batak its meaning is magical, not zoological, symbolizing not a lion but the Nāga or Boru Saniang Naga, the primeval water serpent of Hindu-Buddhist mythology.
Singa images are carved on utensils, medicine containers, jewellery, amulets, coffins, sarcophagi, barns and Batak houses, making it a Batak cultural symbol; on houses it is called singa ni ruma.
The singa's apotropaic use may stem from the Batak Hindu-Buddhist period of the ninth century, linked to the kirtimukha, whose Batak version is the singhamugam.

Suanggi or suangi, also keswange or iwangi, is a malevolent spirit in the folklore of many regions of Eastern Indonesia.

A succubus (plural succubi) is a female demon described in various European folklore as appearing in men's dreams to seduce them.

Repeated encounters lead to sex and can produce a hybrid child called a cambion, but at the cost of the man's mental and physical health, which declines fast until he dies if the succubus keeps courting him.
Historically, belief in succubi was driven by distressing night phenomena, chiefly wet dreams and sleep paralysis.
In medieval Europe a union of an incubus or succubus with a human was thought by some to produce half-demon, half-human children; the legendary magician Merlin was said to be fathered by an incubus.
A succubus may look like a beautiful woman, but a closer look may reveal deformities such as bird-like claws or a serpent's tail.
In later folklore the succubus took the form of a siren.
Through history priests and rabbis, including Hanina ben Dosa and Abaye, tried to curb the succubi's power over people.
Children so begotten, cambions, were thought to be born deformed or more open to supernatural influence.
King James in his treatise Dæmonologie rejects the idea that angelic beings can reproduce.

Years later the younger brother refused a red belt from a mysterious man and tied it to a chestnut tree, which burst into flames, and they realised the man was Sugaar.
Sugaar comes from suge (serpent) and -ar (male), 'male serpent'; the reading su (fire) + gar (flame), 'flame of fire', is considered folk etymology.

The Syrbotae are a kind of giant mentioned in many medieval bestiaries, said to live in Africa and stand about eight cubits tall.
A cubit is the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
In the Tuamotu Rata cycle, Tahiti-tokerau was a water-nymph whom Vahi-vero marries.
She was abducted by Puna, king of the underworld and rescued by her husband, becoming parents of Rata.
Tahoe Tessie is a cryptid said to inhabit the depths of Lake Tahoe, on the border of California and Nevada.
Reports of Tessie date back to the mid-19th century, and it has become a well-known part of local folklore.
One of the earliest accounts dates from 1865, when I.C. Coggin of San Francisco reported a massive serpent-like creature.
The legend is often connected to Washoe beliefs in Water Babies, powerful spirits inhabiting the lake, especially around Cave Rock.
Though some claim Washoe roots, the current form of the legend dates mainly to the 20th century.
Tessie's modern appearance is often compared to Nessie of Loch Ness, with sightings reported regularly since the early 1900s.
One prominent theory holds that the creature could be a giant sturgeon.
According to limnologist Charles Goldman of the UC Davis Tahoe Research Group, many sightings of humps or waves could be caused by wind or water movements.
Tailypo is a creature of North American folklore, particularly in Appalachia.
The Tailypo is usually said to be the size of a dog.
It is nocturnal, covered in dark fur to blend into its environment.
Taka-nyūdō is a tall-monk yōkai of Shikoku and Kinki.
A Hyōgo account places it in narrow sake-brewery alleys.
The creature grows taller as the person looks up, becoming a giant reaching the heavens.
It is compared with mikoshi-nyūdō and Takabōzu.
A Kagawa tradition uses a bow and a saying to make it disappear.
Hyōgo accounts identify it as a transformed tanuki or fox.
Takaonna is a yōkai in Toriyama Sekien’s illustrated book.
Its image shows a woman with an elongated lower body.
Sekien supplied no explanatory text for the picture.
One interpretation considers it a satirical invention from the Edo period.
The talamaur is a vampire legend of the Banks Islands, Vanuatu, in the South Pacific.
A talamaur was a kind of vampire who controlled the ghost of a dead person and could use it to drain the vitality of the living and the recently dead.
Some people actually aspired to become talamaurs; the power was supposedly gained by eating part of a corpse, creating kinship with the soul of the deceased.
A talamaur could be identified by the smoke of certain burning leaves, which made it shout the names of the dead person whose ghost it controlled and of the person it was afflicting.
Injuries to the talamaur's ghostly form appeared on its living body, and such bruises were used to identify a talamaur.
The name talamaur comes from the Mota language of the Banks Islands of Vanuatu and is cognate with Mwotlap na-talmiy.
Both forms descend from Proto-Torres-Banks *tala-mauri, literally "living soul" (*tala "soul", *mauri "to live").
In Mangaian mythology, Tamangori is a legendary giant.
Tamangori is described as over nine feet in height, moving silently and eating humans.
He was killed by two brothers, Pa and Pe, from a village called Ivirua.
Tangie is documented as tangie tongie shape in regional lore.
Taniwha are respected as kaitiaki protective guardians of people and places.
Taotao Mo'na are spirits of ancient giant inhabitants protecting mountains in the Mariana Islands.
Locals believe permission must be requested before entering the jungle or harvesting fruit and wood.
Taowu is a Chinese mythological creature counted among the Four Perils.
Its meaning expanded from a particular beast to mythical beings and stubborn people.
Sima Qian portrays it as a rebellious and destructive son of Zhuanxu.
In the mythology of Mangaia in the Cook Islands, the Tapairu are elves or fairies named after daughters of Miru.
They were said to have been present when mortals danced in honor of their brother, Tau-Titi.
They were also associated with the god Tane.
The tapire-iauara is a legendary creature in the folklore of the Amazon rainforest region.
The tapir-nymph patrols the flooded forest to guard it from humans.
It grows big as a cow and attacks people in boats.
A tarand, also tarandos, tarandus, parandrus or parandros, is a legendary reindeer- or moose-like creature with chameleon-like powers.
It is mentioned by Pliny, Aelian in De Natura Animalium, Solinus and Caesar, and appears again in later texts such as the York Mystery Cycle (1440) and Rabelais's Pantagruel (1552).
Aristotle, Pliny and Aelian place the animal in Scythia, while Solinus puts it in Aethiopia.

According to the Aristotelian text, among the Scythian Geloni there is a very rare beast called tarandus that changes the colour of its hair to suit its surroundings, so it is hard to catch, taking the colour of trees and ground.
The animal is the size of an ox, with a deer-like head.
The truth of the tarand was discussed by Baron Cuvier (1769–1832).
According to the German article it is ox-sized, furred (sometimes long-haired), cloven-hoofed and antlered, and can change its fur colour to camouflage itself.
The reindeer's scientific name, Rangifer tarandus, comes from its name.

Tartaro, Tartalo or Torto of Basque mythology is an enormously strong one-eyed giant much like the Greek Cyclops Odysseus faced, living in mountain caves and catching young people to eat, sometimes sheep too.
Torto, Anxo and Alarabi are the forms listed by Barandiaran, with 'Tartalo' a local variant of the Zegama area.
Cerquand in his 1875 book suggested that the name 'Tartaro' came from the Tartar people.
A magic ring is a common theme in the Tartalo tales.
One day two brothers from the Antimuño farm, out hunting, sheltered from a storm in a cave that turned out to be Tartalo's.
After Tartalo ate the elder brother and fell asleep, the younger stole his ring and drove the roasting spit into his only eye.
Tartalo searched for the boy among his sheep, but the boy put on a sheepskin and escaped.
The ring shouted out his whereabouts and would not come off, so at a cliff edge the boy cut off his finger and threw it down; Tartalo followed the ring's shouts and fell off the cliff.
According to the French article, a figure called Tartari was known beyond Gascony, in the Agenais on the right bank of the Garonne.
His traits and adventures closely match those of the Cyclops Polyphemus: like him he lives in a cave and keeps sheep.
Some sources explain Anxo or Ancho as another name for Basajaun.
According to the Spanish article, his size and appetite are enormous, and his favourite pastime of hurling stones from mountain to mountain is said to have created several structures still standing.
The Tata Duende or El Dueño del Monte is a supernatural creature appearing in cultural folklore stories, mostly evident in Creole cultures.
Tata Duende is considered a powerful spirit that protects animals and the jungle, though it is believed to lack thumbs.
The name Tata Duende comes from the Yucatec Maya word 'Tata' meaning Grandfather or old and the word 'Duende' is Spanish for goblin.
This creature has appeared on a postage stamp of Belize as part of a series on Belizean folklore.
Te Wheke-a-Muturangi is a monstrous octopus destroyed in Tory Channel by Kupe.
The octopus was a pet or familiar of Muturangi, a powerful tohunga of Hawaiki.
Kupe chased the giant octopus across Cook Strait to Tory Channel and cut off its arms with his adze.
Teju Jagua is the first son of Tau and Kerana, one of the seven legendary monsters of Guaraní mythology.
Their first son was a huge lizard with seven dog heads and fire-shooting eyes.
He is considered lord of the caves and protector of fruit.
Tek-ko-kui is a Taiwanese folkloric demon whose name denotes a bamboo ghost.
The tale says bamboo bends to block people passing through its forest.
People stepping over the bamboo are believed to be lifted into the air and injured.
The bamboo stands upright again if the person stops advancing.
Tenawa is a parrot frequently featured in Meitei mythology and folktales of Kangleipak.
Sanagi Tenawa tells of a divine golden parrot making trees speak and move.
A prince and the minister's son set out to bring the parrot to their kingdom.
A tree monster guards the cave entrance and asks the prince to answer questions.
The parrot instructs him to use water from the golden pond to restore princes turned to stone.
When the parrot leaves, the formerly lively trees and bushes become still.
Teng, or Tengshe, is a flying dragon of Chinese mythology.
Tenghuang is an auspicious creature in Chinese mythology.
Tenghuang is mentioned in the Shanhaijing.
One version describes a foxlike beast with wings and dragonlike horns on its back.
Another version gives Tenghuang a horse's appearance; its rider is said to gain a lifespan of two thousand years.
Tengu can be considered yōkai or kami.
In Japanese folk belief, tengu inhabit high mountain woodlands.
Tengu are usually portrayed with human bodies, wings, and sometimes talons.
Karasu Tengu has a birdlike head and sharp beak; Ko no ha Tengu has a human face and very long nose.
Tengu are credited with great strength, flight, shape-changing, and possessing humans.
Tengu are sometimes described as benevolent spirits protecting people or temples.
Older tales portray tengu as enemies of Buddhism who trick priests or burn temples.
Tengu’s image changed; by the Edo period they were also enlisted to help find missing children.
Tenome is a Japanese yōkai illustrated by Toriyama Sekien.
It resembles a blind guildsman with eyes in the palms rather than the face.
Sekien’s illustration supplies no explanatory text.
One tale places an encounter in a Kyoto graveyard.
Tentōki and Ryūtōki are a pair of demonlike figures in Japanese tradition.
Their small-oni appearance symbolizes the Four Heavenly Kings’ victory over evil.
Kōben’s statues at Kōfuku-ji carry lantern offerings for the Buddha.
In Turkic mythology Tepegöz is a one-eyed ogre with an eye on his forehead, a kind of cyclops, appearing in the Book of Dede Korkut, a famous epic of the Oghuz Turks.
In Turkic languages tepe means high or hill and goz means eye; the round opening at the top of a yurt is also called a tepegoz.
In the story an Oghuz herdsman sees a nymph who later gives birth, and finds the monstrous infant, a lump of flesh.
Another source glosses tepe as forehead, so Tepegöz means "eye on the forehead".
The core of its story: Tepegöz drives a man into his cave to eat him, but the man blinds his single eye with a sharp point and escapes wrapped in a sheepskin.
Tesso is a rat-associated yōkai linked to the monk Raigō’s vengeful spirit.
Toriyama Sekien used the name Tesso in an Edo-period illustrated collection.
One tale says Raigō’s requested ordination hall was blocked by a rival temple.
Some written versions turn his resentment into a giant rat that destroys sacred books.
The monstrous rat is described as having a stone-hard body.
Its teeth and claws are compared with iron.
Thardid Jimbo is a cannibal giant in Ngarrindjeri tradition defeated by a hunter's family.
Thayé enter towns at noon or night, and rural villagers in Myanmar say they cause diseases like cholera and smallpox.
The thayé has many faces and bodies, e.g. a pregnant ghost with a fat white body and big ears, or tall and slim ones.
The Black Dog of Newgate is documented as black newgate legend in regional lore.
The Cú Bird is a bird from a Mexican folktale that is unhappy with its looks.
According to the legend, the other birds agreed to give the Cu bird one feather each and asked it to become messenger of the council.
One day the eagle sent the Cu bird to summon others, but it was so entranced by the reflection of its feathers in a lake that it forgot the task.
The dragon (Beowulf) is documented as beowulf battles nemesis in regional lore.
In South Carolina ghostlore, the Gray Man is a ghost reportedly seen on the coast of Pawleys Island, South Carolina, that warns residents of coming severe storms and hurricanes.
Legend holds that the Gray Man is the ghost of a young man traveling from Charleston to see his fiancée in 1822.
It was created by the Diário de Pernambuco in the 1970s military dictatorship to replace and signal censored material.

The Mermaids of Staithes is documented as mermaids staithes mentioned in regional lore.

verified_claims.statement: The Mistress of the Copper Mountain is documented as fairy tale mistress in regional lore.
The Ratman of Southend is documented as ratman southend english in regional lore.
Thinan-malkia is an evil spirit in Aboriginal mythology capturing victims by entangling their feet with nets.
The three-legged crow is an East Asian mythological creature representing the sun.
Chinese tales use Yangwu and Jinwu for the sun crow.
The Shanhaijing includes a reference to the three-legged crow.
The crow in a solar disc appears among symbols on formal imperial garments.
This crow is also portrayed with the Queen Mother of the West.
Ti Malice is a trickster and the nemesis of Tonton (Uncle) Bouki in Haitian folklore.
Ti Malice is clever and guileful, while Uncle Bouki is hardworking but very greedy.
In Senegal, Bouki is a hyena and Malice a hare called "Leuk".
Tiamat is a cosmic ocean paired with Abzu.
Tiamat bears the first divine generation after mingling her waters with Abzu.
Tiamat chooses Qingu as a new consort and grants him the Tablet of Destinies.
Marduk divides Tiamat’s body to form the elements of the cosmos.
Alexander Heidel cautions that Tiamat’s dragon form cannot be established with certainty.
Marduk defeats and kills Tiamat in battle.
Tianlong is a flying dragon in Chinese mythology, with the same name also used astronomically.
Its name combines elements for heaven and dragon.
Its Buddhist senses developed to include heavenly nagas or devas and nagas.
The word tianlong is recorded from the Han period.
Tianma is a flying horse in Chinese folklore, with wings possibly understood metaphorically.
In Western Zhou usage, Tianma also referred to a constellation.
The tale of Tiddalik the frog is a creation story from Australian Indigenous Dreaming Stories.
In some Aboriginal language groups, Tiddalik is known as Molok.
In the creation myth, Tiddalik awoke in Wollombi Valley and drank all available fresh water.
Creatures and plant life everywhere began to die due to lack of moisture.
Nabunum the eel made Tiddalik laugh when he tied himself in comical shapes.
As Tiddalik laughed, the water rushed out to replenish lakes, swamps and rivers.
Tiddy Mun is documented as tiddy legendary spirit in regional lore.

The tikbalang (also Tigbalang, Tigbalan, Tikbalan, Tigbolan) is a Philippine folklore creature lurking in mountains and rainforests; tall, bony, with a horse's head and hooves and limbs so long its knees pass its head when squatting; in some versions it is an aborted fetus sent from limbo.
As horses were not native to the pre-Spanish Philippines, the earliest records of the tikbalang do not specify a horse form.
Plasencia wrote that there were ghosts called vibit and phantoms called Tigbalaang.
Among early Tagalogs, the insult 'Tigbalang ca mandin!' ('You are a wild beast!') described someone whose behaviour was improper.
Juan Francisco de San Antonio's Cronicas (1738-1744) describes the tikbalang as a malevolent mountain being able to take many forms, including horses.
According to the Cronicas, it appeared in the mountains as an old man claiming to be their ancestor, as a horse, or as a monster.
The first document describing the tikbalang as a werehorse is Juan José Delgado's Biblioteca Histórica Filipina (c. 1750).
Delgado notes the Visayans used the name unglo for the same creature.
The tikbalang is linked with dark, lonely, overgrown places such as under bridges, bamboo clumps, banana groves, or atop kalumpang and balete trees.
Tikbalangs scare and mislead travellers, making them return to the same path; wearing a shirt inside out or asking permission aloud is believed to counter this.
Four colonial records show a progression: an undescribed Tigbalaang (1589), a winged, odorous mountain apparition (1613), a multi-form being (c. 1731), and a giant with horse legs (1763).
Some Filipinos still believe tikbalangs inhabit trees as guardians.
Jordan Clark separates the history of the tikbalang's name from the history of its image.
San Buenaventura records a belief that the tigbalang had wings and carried people where it wished; those taken grew weak and died.
The tikbalang is also called Tigbalang, Tigbalan, Tikbalan, Tigbolan or werehorse.
In the mythology of Mangaia in the Cook Islands, Tikokura is a sea-dwelling evil spirit in the shape of a storm wave.
Ngaru determined to try his strength against Tikokura and his shark-like companion, Tumuitearetoka.
He provided himself with a surfboard named Orua (the two).
After eight days and nights, Ngaru threw his surfboard to the monsters, who retired to the deep.
Tilberi is documented as tilberi carrier snakkur in regional lore.
In Māori mythology, tipua or tupua are shape-shifting uncanny spirits with various shapes.
Tipua were associated with natural landmarks, phenomena, trees, and rocks.

The tiyanak (also tianak) is a vampiric creature of Philippine mythology in the form of a toddler or baby, usually a crying newborn in the jungle luring travellers; once picked up it reverts and attacks; it also likes to mislead travellers or abduct children.
Plasencia recorded the belief that a woman who died in childbirth was punished with her child and heard lamenting at night; this was called patianac.
According to Martinez de Zuniga (1803) and San Antonio (1738-44), to counter the patianac the husband stripped naked and brandished a sword until his wife was delivered.
In one version it keeps a baby's shape but grows sharp claws and fangs; in another its true form is a little old man with wrinkled skin and a long beard and moustache.
In the Central Luzon version, especially Pampanga, tiyanak are small nut-brown people floating in the air; in a Mindoro legend it turns into a black bird.
The Mandaya of Mindanao say the tiyanak is the spirit of a child whose mother died before giving birth; a similar Malay being is the pontianak.
With 16th-century Spanish colonization, the tiyanak myth merged with Catholicism: tiyanak became souls of infants who died unbaptized, and today also aborted fetuses returning for revenge.
Those led astray by its cries can break the spell by turning their clothes inside out; loud noises like New Year celebrations are also believed to drive it away.
The patianac account is from Fr. Juan de Plasencia on the Tagalogs (1589).
The Tlahuelpuchi is a legendary vampiric witch of Tlaxcala, Mexico, rooted in Nahua culture.
Thus tlahuelpuchi may mean "glowing haze" or "illuminated youth".
It can shapeshift and sucks the blood of infants at night.
Tlahuelpuchi are born with their curse and learn of it around puberty.
Tlahuelpuchi must feed on blood at least monthly or die.
Garlic, onions and metal repel the tlahuelpuchi.
Toell the Great is documented as toell great sculpture in regional lore.
It appears repeatedly in popular books of the Edo period.
Pictures commonly give it a bamboo hat and a tray.

Add a little horror: dramatic chiaroscuro, thin fog, deep shadows, uncanny atmosphere; benevolent beings stay numinous rather than evil. Features remain readable. One subject. No text, frame, watermark, gore, or invented extra anatomy. Subject: Tofu-kozo of Edo Japanese illustration: small childlike yokai wearing a broad woven bamboo hat and simple kimono, holding a wooden TRAY with one square block of white TOFU plainly visible. Standing alone on a wet dark village lane in rain and mist. Ordinary two eyes, no fangs, no weapons, gentle but uncanny silent gaze.

verified_claims.statement: In Nguni mythology, the tokoloshe is a dwarf-like water spirit.
It is a mischievous and evil spirit that can become invisible by drinking water or swallowing a stone.
Tokoloshes are called upon by malevolent people to cause trouble for others.
Protection includes raising beds off the ground and interventions by traditional healers called sangomas.
The tokoloshe is often referenced satirically to critique the influence of superstitions.

The tooth fairy is a childhood folklore figure in Western and Western-influenced cultures: a child who loses a milk tooth puts it under the pillow or on the bedside table, and the tooth fairy comes during sleep and replaces it with a small payment.
In the Middle Ages English children were told to burn their milk teeth or spend eternity searching for them in the afterlife, and fear of witches was another reason to bury or burn teeth.
In medieval Europe a witch was thought to gain total power over someone by obtaining one of their teeth.
The earliest known record of the tooth fairy tradition itself is a 1908 'Household Hints' item in the Chicago Daily Tribune.
Unlike Santa Claus and the Easter Bunny, few details of the tooth fairy's looks are consistent across versions.
A 1984 study by Rosemary Wells found 74% of respondents thought the tooth fairy female, 12% neither male nor female, and 8% either.
According to the Indonesian article, leaving a tooth under the pillow for the tooth fairy is practised across the Anglosphere.
According to the Japanese article, the tooth fairy (German Zahnfee, French la Petite Souris, Spanish Ratoncito Pérez) exchanges lost milk teeth for coins or gifts.
In Japan a lost upper milk tooth is thrown under the floor and a lower one towards the roof from a veranda or window.
Topielec is documented as tenth chapter book in regional lore.

The toyol or tuyul is an undead infant of Indonesian and Malay folklore, also in other Southeast Asian mythologies, typically summoned by shamans (dukun, pawang, bomoh) through black magic, mainly to rob people, similar to the babi ngepet; it brings luck to its host and misfortune to those it meets.
Toyol (Malay) is tuyul in Indonesian, thuyul in Javanese, kecit in Sundanese; in Thai the male is kuman-thong and the female kuman-lay; a similar Philippine creature is the tiyanak.
The toyol is traditionally a near-naked toddler with sharp teeth and red eyes; the Indonesian tuyul adds green skin and pointed ears and can scale walls and roofs.
The toyol behaves like a playful child fond of sweets, toys and clothes; it is said to steal only half of a person's valuables.
Belief in the toyol serves social functions, including discipline, maintaining hierarchy and warding off outsiders.
The wealthy and successful, even government officials, are often associated with using a toyol.
Such stories are theorized as a way to reduce dissonance, letting people accept status as beyond their control; or simply a way to voice resentment.
Kuman-thong and kuman-lay are said to be more benevolent and, unlike the toyol, need neither sacrifices nor rituals.
In Japanese folklore, the zashiki-warashi resembles the toyol in bringing good fortune to its owners.
The toyol is said to steal only half of a person's valuables.
Toyotama-hime is Watatsumi’s daughter, Hohodemi’s consort, and Ugayafukiaezu’s mother.
Toyotama-hime met Hohodemi in the undersea palace.
Hohodemi returned to land after three years.
Her marriage and motherhood appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.
She requested a birthing hut thatched with cormorant feathers.
She forbade Hohodemi to watch the birth, but he peeped in.
Shamed at being seen in that form, she returned to the sea.
The Kojiki and main Nihon Shoki text differ; the latter says dragon.
Visitors pray at her shrine for health and beautiful skin.
Toyotama-hime marries Hoori in the legend.

The trasgo, trasno or trasgu is a mythological creature in the traditions of several cultures of northern Spain, especially Galician, Asturian and Cantabrian, and also in legends of northern Portugal.
It is a mischievous, restless house goblin, often shown as a tiny man limping on his right leg, dark-skinned, in red clothes and a pointed red hat, with a hole in his left hand.
Night noises and small pranks such as moving objects are blamed on him; he enters homes at night while the household sleeps.
On the other hand, when treated well, he does the housework at night.
In one tale a household moves away because of the trasgu; on the way the wife asks whether they left anything, and the trasgu, following them, answers: 'You left the lamp, but I'm carrying it.'
To get rid of a trasgu one must set him an impossible task, such as carrying sea water in a basket, picking millet off the floor (it falls through the hole in his hand) or whitening a black sheep.
In Asturias the trasgu has different names by place, such as Trasno, Cornín or Xuan Dos Camíos in western Asturias.
The trasgu or trasno is very common in the folklore of Trás-os-Montes and was carried by the Portuguese across their empire, giving rise to similar myths such as the Saci in Brazil.
According to the Spanish article, the name comes from Latin transgredī, 'one who transgresses', and in Galicia he is called trasgo, trasno or tardo.
The Russian article also calls the trasgu the best-known being of Asturian mythology, a mischievous, restless house goblin.
In the Chilote mythology of Chiloé, Chile, the Trauco is a small, dwarf-like humanoid living deep in the forest, with an ugly face and legs without feet.
It is a child of the snake god Coi Coi-Vilu.
It has a strong pull on young and middle-aged women; in myth its wife is the wicked, ugly Fiura.
The Trauco carries a small stone-headed hatchet to strike trees in the forest.
Some men of Chiloé fear the Trauco, believing his gaze can kill.
When an unmarried woman is pregnant and no man claims fatherhood, people assume Trauco is the father, and she is held blameless because he is irresistible.
The Trauco looks like an ugly, ogre-faced man no taller than 80 cm, with stumps instead of feet.
He carries a twisted staff called a pahueldún and a small magic stone hatchet.

The Trenti is an imp-like creature of Cantabrian mythology in northern Spain, an annoying but not malicious goblin that is hard to see because it lives deep in the forest and looks like mushrooms, leaves and moss.
Its most distinctive features are an all-black face and green eyes.
It tends to avoid people but likes jumping out of bushes to scare walkers, and its favourite prank is pulling women's skirts.
Though pranksters, they also secretly help people, especially children, helping shepherds find livestock after storms or the Ojáncanu's mischief, and aiding old women who cannot fend for themselves.
It eats corncobs and sloes but never drinks water, which is poison to it.
According to the Esperanto article, in winter they sleep sheltered in sinkholes and in summer under cool trees.
Tréo-Fall is documented as rocks ushant island in regional lore.
Treuer Eckart is documented as heroic legend eckart in regional lore.
The three-headed eagle is a mythological or heraldic eagle, an augmented version of the double-headed eagle.
A three-headed eagle appears in the apocryphal Latin Ezra, in a dream of the high priest Ezra.
In a Chechen fairy tale a three-headed eagle is a monstrous foe the hero must kill.
Öksökö is an eagle with two or three heads in Yakut and Dolgan folklore.
A three-headed eagle is shown as the arms of minnesinger Reinmar von Zweter (c. 1200–1248) in the Codex Manesse (c. 1300).
The sceptre of Tsar Michael I of Russia was decorated with a three-headed eagle.
In heraldry the three-headed eagle is a rare charge.
The text describes an eagle with twelve feathered wings and three heads rising from the sea.
No one description fits all trolls.
The modern troll sense derives from Old Norse.
Troll can denote jötnar, mountain dwellers and ghosts.
Some tales say church bells drive trolls away.
Old Norse sources describe isolated trolls living in small families.
Trolls may appear grotesque or humanlike.
Folklore links some landmarks to sun-exposed trolls.
Troll cat is documented as troll familiar witch in regional lore.
The Trout Lake Monster is an animal claimed to inhabit Big Trout Lake in northern Ontario.
In 2010, photographs of an unidentified carcass prompted speculation and retellings of local First Nations legends of an animal said to presage bad news.
According to a University of Toronto professor, the animal carcass was likely an ordinary mink in a state of decomposition.
Trow (folklore) is documented as trow drow trowe in regional lore.
The scroll portrays Tsuchigumo as a demon shaped like a giant ground spider.
Yorimitsu and Watanabe no Tsuna pursue a flying skull to Kyoto.
They find monsters in an old house and face a giant creature.
The creature reveals itself as a giant ground spider.
The museum associates the scroll’s painting style with the Kamakura period.
The story is also known in Taiheiki and Noh.
In a kabuki telling, the spider appears as a monk and traps with a web.
In the print, Yorimitsu’s illness is linked to the spider and ends when he kills it.
Tsuchinoko is a thick-bodied snake-like figure said to appear on paths, fields, and riverbanks.
Accounts describe a thirty to eighty centimeter creature with a bottle-thick body.
Reported sightings range from Iwate to Kagoshima.
Tsuchinoko has varied local names and is not a uniform national figure.
Tsuchinoko has not been scientifically confirmed.
Tsuchinoko is described as both a yōkai and a cryptid.
Search events, local products, and bounties turn tsuchinoko into a collective pursuit.
Possible tsuchinoko bones were found in Yoshii in 2000.
A biologist identified the bones as a malformed grass snake.
A news account describes tsuchinoko as a fat snake not conclusively confirmed as real.
Tsukumogami are animate household objects.
In the Muromachi tale Tsukumogami ki, containers, tools, and instruments receive souls after nearly one hundred years.
Folktales describe tsukumogami as tools and other objects that acquire spirits over time.
An object may become a malicious yōkai or benevolent spirit depending on its treatment.
A scholar argues that Tsukumogami ki spread Shingon Buddhist teachings.
Night-parade scrolls show tsukumogami as living objects with limbs.
Prints show animated cups, teapots, ladles, a shamisen, fans, and mochi tools.
The depicted animated objects were familiar items of everyday life.
One furry-legged kettle is a disguised tanuki, not a tsukumogami.
In Japanese folklore, tsukumogami are tools or household objects that acquire a spirit.

verified_claims.statement: The warak ngendog is a mythical creature like a rhinoceros carrying eggs, celebrated at the Dugderan Festival before Ramadan, believed to represent Semarang's Javanese, Chinese and Arab communities; its head is dragon-like (Chinese), its body combines the buraq (Arab) and a goat (Javanese).
The Dugderan highlight is the street parade carrying the warak ngendog (warak ngendhog) through Semarang; its market is held at Johar Market every Sya'ban.
Warak is adapted from the Arabic for holy and ngendog is Javanese for laying eggs; philosophically, warak ngendog is a call to keep oneself pure in Ramadan.
Other readings: warak in Javanese means a horned mythical beast (like a rhinoceros), or comes from buraq, the Prophet Muhammad's mount.
The warak ngendog is covered in upside-down feathers in bright red, yellow and white; its egg lies between the hind legs.
The name Dugderan comes from the drum at the Great Mosque of Semarang (dug) and the cannon (der).
Dugderan reportedly existed by 1881-1889, when Semarang was ruled by Regent Raden Mas Tumenggung Arya Purbaningrat.

He came upon a small adobe hut where a woman had just given birth to twins; she hosted him generously, and he named the children Wars and Sawa and gave her money to build a bigger house.
Later others settled near the house, forming a settlement named after the twins, Warsawa, which became Warszawa, the Polish name of Warsaw.
In a different version Wars and Sawa were a married couple living in that house who hosted the duke.
In another version Sawa was a mermaid living in the Vistula river with whom a fisherman named Wars fell in love.
In yet another version Wars and Sawa were brothers, fishermen living near today's Warsaw Old Town.

In Slavic mythology a werewolf is a human shapeshifter who temporarily takes wolf form; often described as an ordinary wolf with some oddities betraying its human origin, it keeps human intelligence but cannot speak.
The idea is ancient and found among all Slavic peoples, most fully among Belarusians, Poles and Ukrainians; in Russian folklore the figure is often simply called a shapeshifter.
Among Russians the term volkolak is recorded only in southern regions.
In Belarusian, the vaŭkalak or vaŭkalaka is a person turned into a wolf, a shapeshifter.
Sorcerers were believed to turn into wolves by reciting spells and leaping over, stepping over, tumbling through or passing through charmed objects, or draping them over themselves.
To turn back into humans, sorcerers repeated the actions in reverse; they became werewolves on purpose to harm others.
In Belarusian belief, a willed change is made by somersaulting over knives stuck point-up in the ground, from one to twelve in different tales (1, 5, 7, 12).
Some beliefs told of people born prone to periodic shapeshifting because of their parents' deeds or as punishment for their own sins; in human form they showed animal traits such as wolf-like hair.

Such werewolves were thought to lose control in wolf form, attacking livestock and even people, loved ones included, and were sometimes tied to cannibalism; ancient beliefs also linked them with eclipses.
Sorcerers or witches were also believed able to turn a person into a wolf, often in revenge, by bewitching a wolf skin, a belt or a door; a popular tale has a whole wedding party turned into wolves.
Involuntary werewolves suffered fear and despair, longed for human life, avoided real wolves and shunned carrion and raw meat.
The myth probably grew from ancient totemic beliefs and youth initiation rites, and its image may reflect observations of people with physical or mental disorders or of old, sick wolves.

A White Lady (or woman in white) is a type of female ghost, typically dressed in a white dress or similar garment, reportedly seen in rural areas and associated with local legends of tragedy.
Although the details differ, many White Lady traditions share recurring themes of untimely death, grief, betrayal, or unfulfilled love.
Some legends portray her as a silent apparition or an omen of misfortune, while others describe encounters in which she asks travelers for assistance before mysteriously disappearing.
One legend claims that the surroundings of Montmorency Falls near Quebec City are haunted by a white lady.
In Arkansas folklore, the White River Monster is a large creature reportedly first spotted off the banks of the White River near Newport.
Although reported as a monster, it is loved by neighborhood residents and referred to locally as Whitey.
It is illegal to harm the monster inside the refuge.
The Whowie is a fearsome seven-metre long six-legged goanna-like creature with a frog head.
Whowie lived in a cave along the Murray River and his trampling formed sandhills in the Riverina district.
Wiedergänger is documented as core myth concept in regional lore.
Wight is documented as english wiht variously in regional lore.
Wihwin is a malevolent water spirit of Central America, associated especially with the Miskito tribe.
Similar creatures include the kelpie in Scotland, the Scandinavian bäckahäst and the Australian bunyip.
Though normally sea-dwelling, it roams mountain ridges in the summer months.
The horse-shaped monster has jaws of horrid teeth with which it devours humans and other prey on its nocturnal hunts.
Wild haggis is documented as wild haggis given in regional lore.
Will-o'-the-wisps are typically attributed as ghosts, fairies or elemental spirits meant to reveal or conceal a path or direction.
These wisps are portrayed as dancing or flowing in a static form, until noticed or followed, in which case they visually fade or disappear.
The term will-o'-the-wisp comes from wisp, a bundle of sticks or paper used as a torch, and the name Will.
The term jack-o'-lantern originally referred to a will-o'-the-wisp.
Equivalents of will-o'-the-wisps appear in European folklore under names such as ignis fatuus, feu follet, Irrlicht, dwaallicht, and fuoco fatuo.
The phenomenon is known in the United Kingdom by various names including jack-o'-lantern, friar's lantern, and hinkypunk.
In Scottish folklore, will-o'-the-wisps are depicted as mischievous spirits or ghosts of the dead eager to lead travellers off path and to death.
The lights typically appear close to a bog, marsh, or swamp where straying off path can become dangerous or deadly.
Few myths show the will-o'-the-wisps leading those brave enough to follow the light in the dark night to vast treasure.
Some believe the spirits behind will-o'-the-wisps were souls unable to enter Heaven or Hell, forced to wander the earth forever.
In Sweden, the will-o'-the-wisp is a manifestation of an unbaptised soul trying to lead travellers into water in hopes of baptism.
Will-o'-the-Wisp is the most common English designation for fairy-beings characterized by fiery appearance and misleading wayfarers.
The term wisp refers to a twist of straw, used as a torch.
Other names for these apparitions include Hobby-Lantern, Jack-o'-Lantern, Jenny-Burnt-Tale, Kitty-Candlestick, and Peg-a-Lantern.
The Ellylldan is a species of elf exactly corresponding to the English will-o'-wisp.
Wind Horse is a flying-horse image symbolizing the soul in East and Central Asian traditions.
In Tibetan Buddhism, the horse also symbolizes well-being and good fortune.
The term Wind Horse denotes good fortune beyond the flags placed in high locations.
Wirnpa is a rainmaking snake who according to Western Desert legend created the land around Percival Lakes in the Dreaming and repelled outsiders.
Wirry-cow is documented as scotland wirry scots in regional lore.
Witches of Anaga is documented as witches anaga according in regional lore.
Witte Wiwer is documented as witte wiwer mecklenburg in regional lore.
