verified_claims.statement: The World Turtle is a motif of a giant turtle supporting or containing the world.
The motif occurs in Hindu, Chinese, and some Indigenous American traditions.
In Hindu tradition the world turtle is known as Akupara or Chukwa.
The Chinese version tells of Nuwa using Ao's legs to support the sky after Gong Gong damages Mount Buzhou.
The Lenape Great Turtle story was recorded by Jasper Danckaerts in 1678–1680.
In Mackenzie's retelling movement of Kurma's limbs makes Shesha yawn and causes earthquakes.
Worm of Linton is documented as scottish mythical beast in regional lore.
The wulver or wullver is a wolf-like humanoid of the folklore of the Shetland Islands of Scotland, whose origin is now disputed.
The Shetland folklorist Jessie Saxby calls the wulver benevolent, though later accounts say it turned violent if provoked; wulvers were usually friendly to locals and shared the fish they caught.
Saxby wrote that the wulver was like a man with a wolf's head, covered in short brown hair, living in a cave dug into a steep knoll halfway up a hill.
He liked catching and eating fish from a little rock in deep water still called the Wulver's Stane, and often left a few fish on a poor person's windowsill.
Susan Schoon Eberly has speculated the wulver tale may come from people with a medical condition, perhaps Hunter syndrome or lycanthropy.
Others, such as the Shetland Museum archivist Brian Smith, argue the wulver is wholly Saxby's invention and was never part of Shetland folklore.
The Catalan article also calls the wulver a humanoid wolf creature of the folklore of the Shetland Islands off Scotland.
Wuzhiqi is a Chinese supernatural being commonly depicted as a monkey-like aquatic demon.
Poul Andersen identified a Wuzhiqi iron statue at Berlin's Asian Art Museum in 2001.
Some scholars propose it as a model for Sun Wukong, but the figures remain distinct in the novel.
The wyvern or wivern is a kind of mythical dragon with two legs, two wings and often a pointed tail.
Unlike other dragons, the wyvern of heraldry and folklore rarely breathes fire.
The final -n was added by the early 17th century, when John Guillim in 1610 described the 'wiverne' as having a fowl's wings and legs and a serpent's tail.
The medievalist William Sayers proposed that the images of 'venomous snake' and 'light javelin' (guivre) merged into the new idea of a flying snake.
Winged snakes appear across ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern cultures, for example the Egyptian goddess Wadjet, a winged cobra protecting Lower Egypt from Predynastic times.
According to the Indonesian article, depending on the culture the wivern may breathe fire, have deadly venom, both, or neither.
There is a sea variant, the sea-wyvern, with a fish's fin in place of its coiled dragon tail.
According to the Japanese article, outside Britain two-legged dragons are treated as ordinary dragons in Europe; distinguishing them as wyverns is peculiar to Britain and its former colonies.
Some once equated wyvern with Latin viverra, 'ferret', a folk etymology.
The xana is a figure of Asturian mythology, always female and extraordinarily beautiful, believed to live in springs, rivers, waterfalls or forests with pure water.
The origin of xana is unclear, though some scholars derive it from the Latin name of the goddess Diana, and the xanas' homes are still common in Asturian place names.
Xanas promise treasure and can be disenchanted; some also attack people and steal food, and they live in springs and caves.
A xana can be kindly, offering 'love water' to travellers and gold or silver to those judged worthy, and her hypnotic voice is heard on spring and summer nights.
The pure of soul who hear her song are filled with peace and love, while the impure feel smothered and may go mad.
Xanas have children called xaninos, but since they cannot make milk they usually swap a human baby in its cradle for their own fairy child, like changelings elsewhere.

According to the German article, the xana appears as a beautiful young woman who leaves her mountain cave in the morning to bathe in her ice-cold spring, and by oral tradition of the Picos de Europa wishes she hears then come true.
A changeling betrays itself only when eggshells are stacked by the hearth, for it cries in surprise, 'I was born a hundred years ago, but I have never seen so many eggshells by the fire!'
According to the French article, they appear as very beautiful young girls, blonde and light-eyed, combing their hair with golden combs on riverbanks while waiting to seduce travellers.
Xeglun is the celestial elk in Tungusic mythology.
It was Mangi (Xargi)'s pursuit of this creature that was said to have created the Milky Way.
Xeglun is the celestial elk of Tungusic mythology.
Xeglun was the celestial elk referenced in regional mythological accounts.
Belief holds that the cause of the Milky Way was Mangi's pursuit of this creature.
Xelhua is one of seven Aztec giants who escaped the flood by climbing the mountain of Tlaloc and then built the Great Pyramid of Cholula.
He is one of the six giant sons of Mixcoatl, personification of the Milky Way.
Xiao is a name used for several Chinese creatures, including a long armed ape and a four winged bird.
The word xiao includes meanings of noise and clamor.
One Xiao resembles an ape, has long arms, and is skilled at throwing things.
Another Xiao is described as a bird with four wings, one eye, and a dog's tail.
Xiaotian Quan is a Chinese mythological dog accompanying the god Erlang Shen.
It helps Erlang Shen fight demons through its bite and howl.
Some identify it with Tiangou.
It is also identified with Hou Yi's hunting hound.
Xicalancatl (also Xicallancatl or Xicalcoatl) is one of the six giant sons of Mixcoatl and Tlaltecuhtli who populated the Earth after the Great Flood in the Fifth Sun of Aztec mythology.
He was the fourth son, who settled on the coasts of the Gulf of Mexico in the region called Xicallanco.
The six brothers dwell on earth and are the trunk of various races.
In the Lunheng tale, Gao Yao orders it to ram guilty defendants.
The Lunheng also mentions their images painted in public offices.
Chinese dynasties promoted xiezhi as a symbol of traditional law.
The judicial hat was named xiezhi after the mythical sheep or ox.

verified_claims.statement: One account calls Xingtian an official of Yandi continuing resistance against Huangdi.
Chapter seven of the Shanhaijing records Xingtian's resistance.
He uses his nipples as eyes and navel as mouth while dancing with axe and shield.
Luo Mi's Lushi links him to music for farming activities.
Xiuhcōātl was a mythological serpent, the spirit form of the Aztec fire god Xiuhtecuhtli, sometimes shown as an atlatl or weapon of Huitzilopochtli.
Xiuhcoatl is a Classical Nahuatl word meaning "turquoise serpent", and symbolically "fire serpent".
Xiuhcoatl was a common subject of Aztec art, including codices, and appears as a back ornament on images of Xiuhtecuhtli and Huitzilopochtli.
Xiuhcoatl is interpreted as the embodiment of the dry season and was the weapon of the sun.
The royal diadem (xiuhuitzolli) of the Aztec emperors apparently represented the tail of Xiuhcoatl.
Xiuhcoatl was usually shown with a sharply back-turned snout and a segmented body.
Its body was wrapped in knotted paper strips, linking it to bloodletting and sacrifice.
In Aztec mythology Xiuhcoatl personifies the dry season and scorched earth.
In his birth story Huitzilopochtli was born armed from Coatlicue and fought with a shield, darts and Xiuhcoatl.
She is said to dwell in the forest to lure men to their deaths with her incomparable beauty.
She is described as having beautiful, shining black hair that falls down to her ankles and wearing a white dress.
Yacumama (Quechua, "mother of water") is an enormous mythical serpent believed to inhabit the Amazon rainforest.
Legend makes it the mother of all aquatic animals, sucking in any living thing within 100 steps.
For protection, local Indigenous people blew a conch before entering the water, believing the Yacumama would reveal itself.
Yahui is a supernatural figure of mixed animal and human forms in Mixtec culture and belief.
It is an important recurring motif of Mixtec iconography, especially in the pre-Columbian era.
In Postclassic Mixtec codices the yahui wears a serpent tail and headdress and a turtle carapace.
The yahui has two main forms: the nahual (man-animal composite) and the animal figure.
At times the nahual figures hold sacrificial knives and perform rites.
Yakshas are a class of nature spirits in Hindu mythology associated with water, trees, forests, treasure, and fertility.
The female form is called yakshi or yakshini.
A yaksha may be a harmless nature spirit or a ghost that waylays and devours travellers.
Kubera is regarded as king of yakshas in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism.
In Buddhist literature yakshas attend Vaisravana, guardian of the northern quarter.
Mackenzie calls yakshas guardians of hidden treasure associated with Kuvera.
Yali or Vyala is a Hindu creature with a lion body, elephant trunk and tusks, and sometimes equine features.
Yalis become prominent in sixteenth century South Indian sculpture.
Its iconography can include a serpent tail or standing on a makara.
It is regarded as a guardian protecting humans physically and spiritually.
Denmark's National Museum describes the yali as a mythical being with a lion's body and face and an elephant trunk.
Yallery Brown is documented as yallery brown mischievous in regional lore.
Yalungur is a great bird, an eagle or hawk, in the mythology of the Bullanji people.
Yama-uba, also known as yamamba, is a Japanese yōkai.
Yama-uba are female yōkai living in mountain huts.
In some tales she offers lodging as an old or young woman.
Some stories have yama-uba reward those who treat her kindly.
Rosetsu’s painting shows a fearsome yama-uba with her adopted child.
Legend says yama-uba raised the superhumanly strong Kintarō on a mountain in Hakone.
The painting was donated to Itsukushima Shrine in 1797.
Yama-uba appears as a character in a Noh drama.
Yama-uba is often pictured with disheveled hair and ragged clothes.
Utamaro also depicted yama-uba as beautiful women.
In some stories yama-uba transforms and eats sleeping guests.
Yama-uba stories often have her prey on travelers and merchants.
Its name literally means mountain boy.
Stories place it deep in mountain country.
People are said to hear it more often than they see it.
The name is translated as mountain people or woodsman.
Yanagita interpreted them as descendants of a marginalized ancestral population.
Yanagita records related folktales in Tono Monogatari.
Yamata no Orochi is a great serpent whose name means eight-forked snake.
Yamata no Orochi is a mythological monster of Japan described in the Kojiki as an eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent.
The serpent has eight heads and tails, red eyes, and spans eight peaks and valleys.
Orochi ate the couple’s other daughters and would return for Kushinada-hime.
Susanoo made the serpent drunk on rice wine and killed it.
The sword later became one of the three imperial regalia.
One interpretation reads Orochi as the Hii River and its defeat as taming the river for irrigation.
Susanoo descended to the headwaters of the Hi River in Izumo Province.
Some stories identify it as a kappa living in the mountains.
The Wakan Sansai Zue places it deep in the mountains.
That book describes upright walking and human speech.
A common depiction gives it one central eye.
It is said to imitate a variety of noises.
Yaoguai are a diverse category of supernaturally powered beings in Chinese folklore.
The category is associated with transformation and enchantment.
Abilities vary by being and may include illusions, hypnosis, or causing disease.
Tales generally regard yaoguai as dangerous and capable of harmful influence on people.
The Yara-ma-yha-who is a legendary vampiric monster in Southeastern Australian Aboriginal lore.
The Yara-ma-yha-who is said to dwell in fig trees.
Yatagarasu is a three-legged crow from Japanese myth.
The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki portray it as Amaterasu’s servant.
It was sent to guide Jimmu from Kumano to Nara.
Kamigamo tradition says Kamo Taketsunumi took yatagarasu form to guide Jimmu.
Legend says it returned to Kumano Nachi Taisha.
The shrine’s Yatagarasu Stone is said to be its resting form.
Yatagarasu is called a guiding deity and servant of Kumano deities.
The three-legged crow became an emblem of Kumano shrines.
Yatagarasu appears in Japan’s national soccer team logos.
A subsidiary shrine honors Yatagarasu’s resting place.
The account places them in fields in Namegata county.
Seeing them is rumored to bring destruction to a family.
Matachi is said to kill and enshrine them during Keitai’s reign.
A later account has Maro drive them away from construction workers.
Yawkyawk is a female water spirit in the mythology of the Kunwinjku people of Western Arnhem Land.
Yawkyawks live in freshwater creeks, billabongs, and rock pools.
Yawkyawks serve as guardians and protectors of important water sites.
Yee-Na-Pah is a mountain devil spirit girl in Arrernte mythology who marries an echidna spirit man.
In the Navajo creation story, the Diné Bahaneʼ, Yei Tso and his fellow monsters nearly drove early humans to extinction during the time of the Fifth World.
He was eventually defeated by the Hero Twins, who serve as the primary protectors in Navajo tradition.
A Yekyua or "mother animal" is a class of Yakut spirits that stay hidden until the snow melts in spring.
Each yekyua is tied to a particular animal and acts as a familiar spirit protecting Yakut shamans; they are dangerous and powerful, the most dangerous attached to female shamans.
The kind of animal sets a yekyua's strength: dog yekyua are weak, elk yekyua strong; only shamans can see yekyua.
If one shaman kills another's animal, the shaman whose animal died also dies.
When the yekyua fight in spring, their shamans fall ill.
The strongest yekyua is the mammoth.
Yelbeghen is a many-headed man-eating monster in the mythology of the Turkic peoples of Siberia.
In the original myths Yelbegen was a many-headed dragon or serpent-like creature, which over time became a many-headed ogre-like giant.
Some epics feature many Yelbegen with different numbers of heads, children of Altan Sibaldai, "the golden witch", a follower of the underworld's lord, and name a Yelbegen king, Yelmogus.
In an Altai legend Yelbeghen was a seven-headed ogre that took revenge on the Sun and the Moon and used to eat them.
Ülgen shot arrows at Yelbeghen.
In some myths Yilbegän is described as a winged dragon, a serpent-like creature or an ogre-like giant riding an ox with 99 horns.
The Yellow Dragon is the animal-form manifestation of the Yellow Emperor in Chinese mythology.
In Wuxing, this dragon embodies the earth element.
Yeren is an unconfirmed creature described as hairy, human-like, and bipedal.
Reported sightings are especially associated with Shennongjia in Hubei, China.
The article reports that academic surveys failed to find Yeren and records no biological confirmation.
Proposed explanations include mistaken identification of monkeys and fabricated reports.
Written accounts of the Tibetan Yeti legend date to the twelfth century.
Some accounts portray the yeti as a reddish-brown-haired, ape-like biped.
Tibetan tradition has two-legged yetis and larger four-legged ones said to prey on livestock.
In the stories, yetis are believed to inhabit alpine forests below the snow line.
In many stories, the yeti is nocturnal and makes a high-pitched whistle or screech.
Tibetan Buddhist stories feature both kind and malevolent yetis.
Mitochondrial DNA analysis of purported yeti samples supported their identification as local bears.
Researchers associate the yeti legend with local bears while acknowledging uncertainty around the wider stories.
Reports of purported yeti footprints spurred Western climbers' interest in the 1950s.
Nepal issued rules for yeti-seeking expeditions.
Yinglong is a winged dragon and rain deity of ancient Chinese mythology.
Classical texts associate it with the Yellow Emperor and King Yu.
The poem asks what the winged dragon traced on the ground and where seas and rivers flowed.
Yōkai are supernatural beings and phenomena of Japanese folklore, including spirits and monsters.
In Japanese folklore, yōkai includes legendary ghosts, monsters, and spirits.
Yōkai is a broad term with no precise English equivalent.
Yōkai may be depicted as humans with altered features, animals, plants, insects, or household objects.
Yōkai culture appears in picture scrolls and multicolored woodblock prints.
Yōkai, once feared, have also come to be viewed as friendlier presences.
Yōkai appear in media including toys and films.
Today it often means a spirit from Western stories, but it can also refer to Japanese beings.
An older Iwate belief attributed the power to revive the dead to yōsei.
Kijimuna of Okinawa is cited as another fairy-like Japanese being.
They appear at night and chirp like sparrows on mountain trails.
One belief says catching them causes night blindness.
In Wakayama, their presence can indicate a protective wolf.
Other accounts interpret their presence as bad luck.
A regional account says only one traveler in a group hears their call.
The Yowie is an Australian folklore entity living in the Outback with roots in Aboriginal oral lore.
In parts of Queensland it is termed a Quinkin or joogabinna.
In New South Wales it is known by names such as Ghindaring, Jurrawarra, and Doolaga.
The Ypotryll is a medieval European chimeric creature of heraldry with a tusked boar's head, a humped camel's body, the legs and hooves of an ox or goat and a long scaly serpent's tail.
Little is known of its meaning or origin, but it is the badge of John Tiptoft, 1st Earl of Worcester, called the "Butcher of England".
Tiptoft was beheaded by the Lancastrians in 1470 during the Wars of the Roses.
Ysätters-Kajsa is documented as kajsa wind troll in regional lore.
Ysbaddaden is documented as ysbaddaden bencawr ysbaddaden in regional lore.
Ysgithyrwyn is documented as ysgithyrwyn chief boar in regional lore.
Yuki-onna is a Japanese yōkai without a single definitive story.
The name Yuki-onna means snow woman.
Yuki-onna stories occur in snowy parts of Japan and have regional variants.
Yuki-onna is often depicted with white skin and a white kimono.

verified_claims.statement: Yumboes are supernatural beings in the mythology of the Wolof people of Senegal, West Africa.
Their alternative name Bakhna Rakhna literally means good people.
Yumboes are spirits of the dead with a pearly-white complexion.
The Yumboes live beneath the Paps hills and dance in the moonlight.
They feast on large tables waited on by servants invisible except for hands and feet.
They invite both natives and foreigners to their feasts.
Sawaki Suushi’s 1737 Hyakkai Zukan includes this figure.
The figure has the appearance of a very thin old man.
His loose white clothing leaves the ribs visible.
He has flowing sparse hair.
He carries a cane and beckons with his other hand.
His lower body appears to fade away.
Yuqiang is a deity of the north sea and wind in Chinese mythology.
Accounts identify him as a Yellow Emperor descendant and Yuhao's son.
Some Shanhaijing accounts give him a bird body and human face, with serpents supporting his feet in travel.
Yūrei is the spirit of a deceased person.
The meaning of the Japanese word yūrei changed over the centuries.
Yūrei may remain in the human world for personal reasons or insufficient funeral rites.
In art and literature yūrei are often shown as long-haired women in burial clothes, with dangling hands and no feet.
In ancient and medieval Japan, yūrei usually meant souls of the dead who neither appeared nor cursed.
Around the fifteenth century, yūrei began to mean resentful spirits.
In the Edo period, people believed a bad relationship in life could lead to revenge after death.
In the later Edo period, yūrei appeared in kabuki and inspired ukiyo-e artists.
In the Edo period, ghost stories became popular and artists painted yūrei.
Yuxa is a legendary creature of Turkic mythology; in popular belief every 100-year-old snake becomes a Yuxa, and in fairy tales it is a beautiful maiden who marries men to have children.
Yuxa has a dragon's head said to breathe fire or bite venomously, a reptilian body, two legs (sometimes none) and a barbed tail.
It can become a handsome young man or beautiful young woman to seduce, protect or frighten people as it pleases.
In Bashkir and Tatar mythology Yuxa is an evil demon linked with water.
Yuxa appears in fairy tales, the epic Ural-batyr and folk beliefs.
In other beliefs, an ajdaha that lives 500 to 1000 years turns into a Yuxa.
Bashkir keeps figurative expressions with Yuxa, such as yukha yylan for a treacherous person.

Zapam Zucum is a dark-skinned, white-handed goddess of the Aymara and Diaguita of northern Argentina, Chile and Bolivia.
She is considered the protectress of the algarrobo tree.
When the goddess dwells in the tree, the sound "Zapam... Zucum" is heard and the children stave off hunger.
She guards the sacred algarrobo; hearing an axe chopping it, she abducts the logger.
She protects baby and young animals from predators and hunters.
Zashiki-warashi is described as a household deity that looks like a child.
The Tōno stories come from mountainous Iwate.
Another account places this child spirit in rooms or storehouses.
Homes with zashiki-warashi are believed to thrive.
Its departure is believed to bring poverty.
An Iwate guide calls it a boy-shaped guardian spirit of the house.
Yanagita Kunio published the Tōno story collection in 1910.
An inn says the spirit lives in Enju-no-Ma and that those who see it succeed.
The tourism guide reports claimed sightings while calling it a legend.

A Buddhist tradition links the dragon with Kūkai’s rainmaking rite in 824.
The name includes an expression meaning dragon king.
Art represents the deity as a small dragon or as a human with a dragon’s tail.
Zheuzhyk is documented as zheuzhyk belarusian creature in regional lore.
Zhulong is a giant red dragon and solar deity in Chinese mythology.
He is portrayed with a human face and a serpent's body.
Opening and closing his eyes produces day and night, while breathing produces seasonal winds.
The Chu Ci contains name variants Chuolong and Zhuolong.
The names Zhuyin and Zhulong occur in Han-period classical texts.
The Shanhaijing gives parallel accounts of Zhuyin and Zhulong.
Zhytsen is documented as zhytsen belarusian positive in regional lore.
Zilant is a legendary creature between a dragon and a wyvern in Tatar mythology.
Since 1730 Zilant has been the official symbol of Kazan, capital of the Republic of Tatarstan in Russia, and this winged snake appears in legends of Kazan's founding.
The Zilant is a fabulous winged snake with the forepart of a dragon, part of Tatar and Russian folklore.
The Zilant differs from Aq Yılan ('White Snake'), the king of snakes.
Despite its bird-like posture, the Zilant differs from the basilisk in having a dragon's head, not a bird's.
A zitiron, or sea knight, is a mythological creature that has an upper body in the form of an armed knight, fused with the tail of a fish.
A zitiron is a medieval mythological marine creature, half-fish and half-armed knight.
The zitiron appears in De natura rerum by Thomas de Cantimpré, written around 1240.
It was included in Jacob van Maerlant's Der Naturen Bloeme in 1350.
It is also found in the Hortus sanitatis, printed in 1491.
It has rough and hard skin, bears a shield, and has thick arms with only two fingers.
It cannot be killed with arrows, but only with hammers, protecting itself with its shield.
Zmei (Russian folklore) is documented as meaning serpent form in regional lore.
Zmeu is documented as zmeu plural zmei in regional lore.
Duyvendak questions interpreting a Classic of Poetry poem as a reference to the Zouyu animal.
Accounts describe it as a righteous animal appearing under a benevolent ruler.
Zouyu appears fierce like a tiger but is gentle and strictly vegetarian.
In 1404, Zhu Su sent a creature described as Zouyu to the Yongle Emperor.
Some modern authors propose the giant panda as the animal identified as Zouyu.

verified_claims.statement: Zwodziasz, also called zwodzijos (in Sieradz), is a devilish creature of Slavic mythology said to lead people astray and lure them into wasteland until they lose their way, often indirectly causing their sudden death.
In tales of people from Kalisz and its surroundings, the zwodziasz is portrayed as a nightjar.
